items.fullDescription: Call for Papers From its inception, cinema has transcended borders through the movement of people, capital, narratives, and visual technology. However, over the past two decades, the term transnational cinema has evolved into one of the most influential and contested frameworks in film studies. Scholars such as Elizabeth Ezra, Terry Rowden, Deborah Shaw, Will Higbee, and Song Hwee Lim have variously expanded, critiqued, and redefined the concept, emphasizing its aesthetic, political, and industrial dimensions and prompting new questions about its theoretical and pedagogical implications. While these approaches have illuminated the circulation of films, filmmakers, and spectators across borders, they have also raised questions about the continuing relevance of the national cinema framework and the analytical boundaries of the transnational itself. This symposium revisits the concept of transnational cinema at a moment when two distinct currents seem bound for collision. On the one hand, global migration, digital media, the global climate catastrophe, geopolitical conflicts, and transregional collaborations have blurred distinctions between the local and the global, as well as the national and the transnational. On the other hand, isolationism, authoritarianism, and protectionism have re-erected physical and ideological borders across the globe. Is the world more or less transnational as a result of these competing impulses? We invite proposals that address theoretical, historical, or pedagogical questions, such as: How can the familiar concept of transnational cinema elucidate emergent and unfamiliar problems in the contemporary landscape? How do we define and teach transnational cinema now? Is transnational cinema best understood as a framework, an approach, a mode of filmmaking, or a category of world cinema? How does transnational cinema intersect with, or diverge from, national, world, and global cinema theories? What are the political, aesthetic, or ethical stakes of emphasizing transnationality in film studies today? We welcome both theoretical interventions and case studies from diverse regions and traditions. Possible topics include, but are not limited to: • Theories and definitions of transnational cinema • Pedagogical approaches to transnational cinema • Feminist, queer, and trans approaches to transnational cinema • Transnational authorship and stardom • Memory, trauma, and postmemory in transnational film • Digital technologies and virtual transnational spaces • Streaming platforms and global distribution • Cinemas of diaspora, exile, and migration • Cross-border activism and solidarity through film • Environmental and ecological transnationalism • Film policy, censorship, and cultural diplomacy • Transnational labor, precarity, and creative economies • International film festivals and global circulation • Archival and historiographical approaches to transnational film • Politics of translation, dubbing, and subtitling • Regional and transregional filmmaking practices • Anti-colonial, postcolonial, and de-colonial aesthetics and narratives • Global Hollywood and transnational co-productions• Transnational spectatorship and global audiences • State, statelessness, and belonging in transnational cinema • Borders, border-crossings, and redefinitions of home • Transnational genres • De-Westernizing film studies Presenters will be invited to submit completed papers for consideration in an edited collection or special issue developed from the symposium. Proposals (250-300 words) and short bios (100 words) should be submitted by June 1st, 2026, using this Google Form: https://forms.gle/R7Jw98KpMEc7BAHo6 For questions, please contact the organizing committee at ahtfilmstudies@utdallas.edu.

items.fullDescription: From Christopher Strachey's Love Letter Generator to today's generative AI writing tools and multimodal models, AI technologies are reshaping how literary works are created, adapted, and circulated across media. Texts can now be generated, illustrated, voiced, animated, and transformed into comics, audiobooks, visual art, and video, prompting renewed questions about creativity, form, authorship, authenticity, and human agency. This seminar asks: Can AI-generated literature and art be understood as forms of artificial creativity? Does AI expand, automate, or redefine human creativity? How does human-AI collaboration challenge traditional ideas of authorship and authenticity? How do generative technologies reshape intertextuality, intermediality, and the boundaries between literature and other art forms? What methodological problems arise when AI is used to analyze AI-generated literature? And how do readers, critics, publishers, and institutions respond differently to AI-generated works across literary genres and fields? We welcome papers on AI-generated literature and multimodal works, human-AI collaboration, authorship and creativity, AI-assisted literary research, intertextuality and intermediality, and literary or artistic representations of AI. To submit a paper proposal, please visit the ACLA seminar page and click "Propose a Paper": https://www.acla.org/seminar/dfc44a1b-7299-4016-a661-6095054a6917 Submission deadline: September 20, 2026. For inquiries, please contact Xuezhao Li (li.11365@osu.edu) or Peizhen Wu (peizhenwu@outlook.com).

items.fullDescription: About the Symposium The Weight of Mountains (TWOM) Symposium 2026 is an international academic symposium in film and media studies, with a primary focus on Vietnamese and Southeast Asian screen cultures and on how cinema documents, reimagines, and gives form to the region's landscapes, urban transformations, and contested histories. Co-hosted by RMIT University Vietnam and Fulbright University Vietnam, the symposium brings together scholars from film studies and audiovisual studies, cultural studies, environmental humanities, postcolonial studies, and related fields to examine cinema's engagement with place, memory, and environment in an era of rapid urbanization and ecological change. The symposium underscores the significance of authorial and experimental film practices and of speculative fiction emerging in our region. The symposium is organised in conjunction with the fourth iteration of The Weight of Mountains, a periodic international film residency and research platform whose 2026/2027 program places international filmmakers in residence in Ho Chi Minh City for three months. This urban turn - situating the residency in a city shaped by colonial histories, wartime trauma, ??i M?i transformations, and accelerating development - provides the occasion for a focused scholarly conversation about cinema's relationship to place, history, and environment in Vietnam and the wider Southeast Asian region. The symposium will feature keynote addresses by leading Vietnamese and international scholars, artist presentations by TWOM resident filmmakers, and presentations of selected papers. Partners include: The Weight of Mountains (TWOM) team, RMIT Vietnam (DFV and SCD), Fulbright University Vietnam (Arts & Media Studies), Trigger Film Academy Call for Abstracts: Ho Chi Minh City is a city of layered temporalities - part and contemporary - and Vietnamese cinema has long been one of the most searching instruments for reading those layers. The city itself operates as a cinematic text: its streets and interiors producing divergent spatial imaginaries shaped by who holds the camera and from where they look. Like in Tran Anh Hung's Cyclo, urban space can be a site of the uncanny and memories, the promised land, or the space of autoreflective questions. Drawing on Guy Debord's psychogeography and Timothy Cresswell's understanding of place as practiced and performed, we ask how filmmakers navigate, intervene in, and reimagine the urban and ecological spaces of the region through experimental narratives, tools and future-oriented imaginaries. Contemporary film studies has been decisively shaped by the turn toward critical transnationalism, insisting on interrogating the uneven power relations, industrial infrastructures, and cultural politics that condition the movement of films, filmmakers, and capital across borders. For Vietnamese and Southeast Asian cinemas, this means attending simultaneously to inter-Asian circuits of production and distribution, to festival economies and co-production networks, and to the diasporic communities whose experiences and investments shape what gets made and how it travels. The Weight of Mountains residency operates as what Foucault called a heterotopia - a space of productive dislocation and otherness, deliberately positioned at the margins of dominant film cultures. This symposium extends that heterotopic logic into the academic register, asking what forms of knowledge become possible when international filmmakers and researchers engage seriously with the specific textures of Vietnamese urban life: its soundscapes, its landscapes and ecologies as sites of historical sedimentation and environmental change, and its postcolonial politics of the gaze. The symposium is equally attentive to what cinema can do when it turns toward the nonhuman world - the Mekong Delta, the urban waterways, the forest edges and street ecologies that constitute the lived environment of Vietnam and the wider region, bringing further questions about how film documents landscape, registers environmental change, and attends to the nonhuman dimensions of place. Thematic Strands We invite submissions that engage with one or more of the following strands. Papers should present a clear research question, theoretical framework, and original contribution to the field. STRAND 1. Colonial and Postcolonial Cinemas of Southeast Asia Vietnamese and Southeast Asian cinemas carry the unresolved weight of French colonialism, Cold War intervention, and the ongoing politics of decolonial representation. Papers in this strand might address: • The postcolonial gaze and ethics of representation in Vietnamese documentary and fiction film • French colonial cinema in Indochina and its afterlives in contemporary Vietnamese film culture • Decolonial aesthetics and counter-narratives in Vietnamese, Cambodian, Lao, and Thai cinema • The postcolonial condition of Indochinese cinemas across Vietnam, Cambodia, and Laos, and the shared legacies of French colonialism • Colonial urban space and its cinematic re-inscription in Ho Chi Minh City, Phnom Penh, and Vientiane • The ethics of the outsider filmmaker in Vietnam and Southeast Asia - questions of access, positionality, and the politics of cross-cultural representation STRAND 2. Memory and the Afterlives of 1975 Post-1975 Vietnamese cinema remains one of the most contested sites of historical memory in world cinema. Papers in this strand might address: • Historical voices in post-1975 Vietnamese film • Wartime affect in Vietnamese cinema • Heterogeneous temporalities, colonial haunting, and the fantastic in Southeast Asian cinema • Uncanny urban spaces • Generational shifts in the remembrance of war and revolution across Vietnamese film STRAND 3. Transnational Return Papers in this strand might address: • Transnational desire, mobility, and national belonging • The aesthetics of displacement, longing, and return in film • Insider and outsider representations of Vietnam and the returning gaze • Transnational co-productions and festival circulation • Digital platforms, streaming, and new circuits of Vietnamese film distribution STRAND 4. Urbanism and the Cinematic City Ho Chi Minh City and Hanoi are among the most cinematically rich urban environments in contemporary Southeast Asia, shaped by ??i M?i reforms, rapid development, and the layering of colonial and socialist pasts. Papers in this strand might address: • Ho Chi Minh City as cinematic city-text • Psychogeography, the dérive, and spatial practice in Vietnamese urban cinema • Postcolonial urbanism and the layering of colonial and contemporary temporalities in Vietnamese cityscapes • Rural-urban boundaries and migration narratives in contemporary Vietnamese cinema • Bangkok, Manila, Phnom Penh, and other Southeast Asian cities as sites of cinematic spatial inquiry • Infrastructural development, displacement, and the politics of urban transformation on screen STRAND 5. Independent Cinema and Alternative Exhibition in Southeast Asia Beyond mainstream production, a vital ecosystem of independent and experimental cinema has emerged across the region, creating alternative circuits of production, distribution, and spectatorship. Papers in this strand might address: • Critical transnationalism and the conditions of production, funding, and circulation of Southeast Asian independent film • Alternative film exhibitions • Independent film festivals and independent production circuits across Southeast Asia • The role of digital platforms and transnational funding in enabling independent Southeast Asian filmmaking • Distinct regional independent cinema identities • The sonic and haptic dimensions of place in experimental Southeast Asian films STRAND 6. Landscape, Ecology, and Environmental Cinema This strand invites scholarship on how cinema represents, interprets, and attends to the landscapes, ecologies, and natural environments of Vietnam and Southeast Asia. It encompasses documentary, essay film, and fiction practices that attend to environmental change, rural and riverine life, and the nonhuman world as subjects of serious cinematic inquiry. Papers in this strand might address: • Landscape cinema and ecocinema studies in the Vietnamese and Southeast Asian context - how films document, aestheticise, and bear witness to environments under pressure • The Mekong Delta as cinematic space - rivers, deltas, and rural waterways as subjects of documentary, fiction, and experimental filmmaking • Climate cinema and the Anthropocene in Southeast Asian documentary and fiction film • Sensory and immersive cinema - the use of duration, texture, and ambient sound to render nonhuman environments perceptible • Process cinema and the nonhuman agencies - water, weather, infrastructure, animals - that constitute urban and rural life in Vietnam and the region STRAND 7. Festival Aesthetics, Slow Cinema, and Global Circulation The growing international visibility of Vietnamese and Southeast Asian cinema raises important questions about the institutional and aesthetic conditions of that visibility. Papers in this strand might address: • Transcendental style, slow cinema, and contemplative aesthetics in contemporary Vietnamese film • The construction of "Vietnamese cinema" as a category within global film culture • Co-production networks, international funding, and the shaping of film form for global audiences • The tension between local spectatorship and international festival circuits in Vietnamese and Southeast Asian cinema • Transnational frames for Asian cinema and the risks of Orientalist programming logics • The role of film criticism, academic writing, and scholarly publishing in shaping the international reception of Southeast Asian cinema SUBMISSION GUIDELINES Abstract requirements: - Word count: 300-500 words, excluding references - Language: English Abstracts should include: - Paper title - 3 to 5 keywords - Indication of which thematic strand(s) the paper engages - Author name(s), institutional affiliation(s), bio note and email address(es) should be provided only in the submission form - Please indicate your presentation format: online/face to face in the form Author biography: A short biography of 100-150 words per author should be submitted alongside the abstract Presentation format: A 20-minute academic paper presentation, followed by 10 minutes for questions and discussion Review process: All submissions will undergo blind peer review by an international panel of scholars. Selection criteria include intellectual rigour, theoretical sophistication, methodological clarity, engagement with Vietnamese and Southeast Asian contexts, and relevance to symposium themes. Authors should remove identifying information from the abstract document prior to submission Submission portal: https://cmt3.research.microsoft.com/TWOM2026/Submission/Index Symposium format: The symposium will have a hybrid format. An additional online session will be held for online participants. KEY DATES: Abstract submission deadline: September 15, 2026 Notification of acceptance: October 2026 Full text submission: November 20, 2026 Symposium: December 10, 11, and 12, 2026 Symposium Venues: -December 10, Online -December 11, RMIT Unviersity, Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam -December 12, Fulbright University, Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam Abstract submissions: https://cmt3.research.microsoft.com/TWOM2026/Submission/Index Please submit the abstracts through the submission system. *Some users encountered problems while using Safari browser. If you have problems with registering, please use a different browser. Registration details to be announced. Please contact the organising committee for queries regarding accessibility requirements. The organizers plan to publish an edited monograph containing expanded, selected articles submitted to the symposium. Details to be announced. items.fullDescription: CALL FOR PAPERS / COLLEGE ENGLISH ASSOCIATION ANNUAL CONFERENCE APRIL 1-3, 2027 / ST LOUIS, MO SUBMISSION SITE IS OPEN: https://www.conftool.pro/cea2027 DEADLINE: 11/01/2026 For its 2027 annual conference,the College English Association (CEA) invites proposals for papers and panels that explore the theme of "Gateways" and their significance in literature, criticism, and pedagogy. we also encourage proposals on GENERAL TOPICS, including AMERICAN, BRITISH, AND WORLD LITERATURES. DON'T KNOW CEA? YOU SHOULD! In December 1938, a group of young academics attending the MLA convention in New York took on the biggest name in their field-the MLA. They chose to forge a new path by organizing into the College English Association and offering a voice to "the college English teachers of America." Their aim was to upend the scholar-teacher dynamic by recognizing teaching as paramount. Today, more than eight decades later, the CEA continues in that same spirit. At our core, we strive to meet these goals through two venues: our Annual CEA Conference and our journal, The CEA Critic. With over 400 active members and a collection of regional affiliates, the CEA welcomes teacher-scholars at all levels-from graduate students to emeritus faculty-who share our belief that teaching is central to who we are and what we do. CEA WELCOMES GRADUATE STUDENTS As always, the CEA extends a special invite to students pursuing a graduate degree, not only to attend the conference but to submit their presentations to the CEA Outstanding Graduate Student Paper competition. The award carries a grand prize of $250 and publication of the winning essay in the CEA's flagship journal, THE CEA CRITIC. NEW FOR 2027:UNDERGRADUATE ROUNDTABLES CEA invites undergraduates to enjoy the conference experience by sharing their work in flash-essay roundtable sessions. A flash essay is a highly condensed, high-impact presentation (typically 300-1000 words, or 2-5 minutes) that delivers core research findings, a specific argument, or a compelling narrative. During roundtable sessions, the speakers and audience engage in discussion with each other in more of an open conversation than in traditional panels. Learn more about roundtables here: https://cea-web.org/about-roundtables. LEARN MORE: https://cea-web.org/cea-2027-%2F-st-louis

items.fullDescription: CFP: Let's Dance: Musicals, Dance, Bodies and Popular Culture PopCRN Online Conference 26-27 August 2027 Popular culture dances. Across stages and screens, ballrooms and nightclubs, streets and stadiums, dance has produced some of popular culture's most enduring images of bodies in motion. From musicals and music videos to television, theatre, popular music and sport, dance crosses cultural forms and national boundaries, continually reinventing how bodies move, perform and become visible. Dance is rarely only entertainment. Dancing bodies carry meanings about beauty, sexuality, gender, race, class, youth, age, disability, nation and cultural identity. They can communicate desire, resistance, freedom and belonging, while also being trained, disciplined, watched, judged and commodified. Popular culture determines which bodies appear graceful or awkward, desirable or excessive, disciplined or unruly, and which bodies are permitted to occupy the centre of the floor. The history of popular dance is therefore also a history of inclusion, exclusion and cultural ownership. Dance forms emerge from particular communities before travelling between cultures, nations and media. Movement can preserve cultural memory, assert identity and create community, but it can also be appropriated, commercialised and detached from the people who created it. These histories raise questions about who creates movement, who owns it, who profits from it and whose contributions remain visible. Dance also makes power visible through the body. Behind apparently effortless performance lie labour, repetition, discipline, endurance and sometimes pain. Ideas of technical perfection, beauty, athleticism and bodily control shape who is recognised as a dancer and how dancing bodies are valued. Dance can reinforce expectations surrounding gender, race, class, age, size and ability, while also providing a means of challenging them. The dance floor can be a political and social space. Dance creates communities, produces collective identities and allows bodies to occupy spaces from which they may otherwise be excluded. Social dance, club cultures, street dance and dance crazes transform audiences into participants and make movement part of everyday popular culture. Dance can be intimate and collective, regulated and rebellious, commercial and political. Who leads, who follows, who watches, who judges and who is allowed onto the floor all matter. Dance continually crosses boundaries between cultural forms. Choreography moves between theatre and cinema, popular music and music video, television and digital media, concert performance and sport. At its largest scale, it transforms individual bodies into mass spectacle, bringing together celebrity, commerce, national identity and collective participation. These crossings also unsettle distinctions between dance, athleticism, performance and entertainment. Let's Dance: Musicals, Dance, Bodies and Popular Culture invites papers exploring dance as representation, performance, narrative, labour, pleasure, identity and embodied politics. We welcome historical and contemporary approaches across film, television, theatre, literature, popular music, sport, celebrity culture, digital media and everyday life. We are particularly interested in intersectional approaches considering how race, gender, sexuality, class, age, disability, nation and cultural identity shape who dances, how bodies are represented and what movement is permitted to mean. The conference asks how popular culture teaches us to understand the dancing body. What happens when movement crosses racial, cultural and national boundaries? How are dancing bodies disciplined, sexualised, celebrated, ridiculed or excluded? When does dance create community, and when does it reinforce hierarchy? Who owns movement and choreography? Who gets to dance for the nation? What happens when bodies expected to remain at the margins claim the centre of the floor? At its centre, Let's Dance asks one overarching question: who gets to dance, and what can the dancing body tell us about power, identity and belonging in popular culture? Possible papers might include: Making the Dancing Body: training, rehearsal and discipline; virtuosity and amateurism; bodily labour, pain and endurance; beauty and perfection; the professional dancer; auditions and competition; the ageing dancing body; The Red Shoes (1948), A Chorus Line (1975 stage musical, 1985 film), Fame (1980), Black Swan (2010) and Dance Moms (2011 to 2019). Race, Culture and Ownership: Black dance traditions and popular culture; tap, jazz and segregation; Lindy Hop and the Savoy Ballroom; disco and ballroom culture; breaking and hip hop; Indigenous dance and cultural sovereignty; Bollywood and diaspora; appropriation, ownership and cultural memory; Stormy Weather (1943), West Side Story (1961, 2021), Paris Is Burning (1990), Pose (2018 to 2021) and Hamilton (2015). Gender, Sexuality and Desire: the dancing female body; dancing masculinity; queer dance cultures; drag, camp and performance; sexualisation and respectability; gender transgression; romance and bodily intimacy; Gentlemen Prefer Blondes (1953), Saturday Night Fever (1977), The Rocky Horror Picture Show (1975), Dirty Dancing (1987), Billy Elliot (2000), RuPaul's Drag Race (2009 to present) and Barbie (2023). Class, Work and Social Mobility: dance as labour; working class dancing bodies; dance and fantasies of escape and mobility; professional ambition; unemployment and masculinity; elite and popular dance cultures; unequal access to training and opportunity; Saturday Night Fever (1977), Flashdance (1983), The Full Monty (1997), Billy Elliot (2000), Step Up (2006) and Swing Time (2016). Who Gets to Dance?: age, disability, body size and bodily difference; exclusion and belonging; normative ideals of the dancer; humiliation and judgement; visibility and the right to perform; Hairspray (1988, 2007), The Full Monty (1997), Billy Elliot (2000), Finding Your Feet (2017), Dumplin' (2018) and Wicked (2024). Dance Floors and Dancing Together: ballrooms, nightclubs, streets, schools, weddings and stages; social dance and dance crazes; dancing alone and together; dance floors as spaces of freedom, desire and exclusion; and collective pleasure; The Twist (1960), Footloose (1984), Strictly Ballroom (1992), Pose (2018 to 2021) and Dancing Queen (1976). Dance, Politics and Protest: dancing as resistance; regulation and censorship; race and segregation; religion and morality; national identity; protest choreography; public space and collective movement; Dancing in the Street (1964), Footloose (1984), Hairspray (1988, 2007), Sarafina! (1992) and Hamilton (2015). From Stage to Screen: vaudeville and the Hollywood musical; Busby Berkeley and mass choreography; Fred Astaire and Ginger Rogers; Gene Kelly and dancing masculinity; the decline and revival of the screen musical; choreography across theatre, cinema and television; Singin' in the Rain (1952), Moulin Rouge! (2001), Chicago (2002), Glee (2009 to 2015), La La Land (2016) and Wicked (2024). Dance on Television: dance and the construction of youth culture; Black dance and cultural visibility; television variety and the spectacular body; reality television, competition and judgement; amateur and professional dancers; drag and choreographed gender performance; musical television and belonging; American Bandstand (1952 to 1989), Soul Train (1971 to 2006), Solid Gold (1980 to 1988), Dancing with the Stars (2004 to present), So You Think You Can Dance (2005 to present), RuPaul's Drag Race (2009 to present). Dance, Celebrity and Mass Spectacle: music video and the choreographed pop star; concert performance and celebrity bodies; cheerleading and athletic spectacle; stadium choreography; bodily endurance and audience participation; Michael Jackson's Thriller (1983), Madonna's Vogue (1990), the Super Bowl halftime show (1993 to present as a major pop spectacle), Bring It On (2000), Beyoncé's Homecoming (2019), Taylor Swift's The Eras Tour (2023 to 2024) and breaking at the Paris 2024 Olympic Games. Dance Across Popular Culture: dance in film, television, theatre, literature, popular music and music video; dance memoir and fiction; reality television and competition; songs about dancing; advertising and celebrity culture; digital choreography, viral dances and social media; the circulation of movement between media, communities, bodies and audiences; and the changing boundaries between dance, sport, spectacle and everyday cultural practice. Registration is free. The conference is welcoming of early career researchers, postgraduates, Indigenous scholars, people with diverse identities, and industry experts or food practitioners. items.fullDescription: Call for Proposals Transformative Synergies Harmonizing the Future: Interdisciplinary Pathways for a Resilient Society Transformative Synergies brings together faculty, scholars, graduate students and practitioners to explore how disciplines can intersect to address the complex challenges shaping our world. As technology, public health, social policy, education and the arts continue to evolve, meaningful solutions increasingly require collaboration across traditional academic boundaries. This conference invites researchers and creators to examine the connections among arts, business, STEM, health and education and consider how these fields can work together to build a more resilient society. Submit Your Work We welcome proposals that explore innovative ideas, research and creative approaches related to the conference theme, including: Pedagogy for a New Era: Interdisciplinary curriculum design, trauma-informed education and the future of the R2 research institution Creative Technologies: Digital preservation, emerging technologies and the ethics of the human-machine interface Social Equity & Policy: Research addressing systemic health and educational disparities Health-Arts Nexus: Narrative medicine, art therapy and the role of the humanities in public health Sustainability & STEM: Environmental science, Indigenous knowledge and resilient urban design These topics are not exhaustive. Proposals that explore meaningful connections across disciplines are encouraged. Graduate Student Symposium The conference will feature a Graduate Student Panel designed to give emerging scholars an opportunity to share research in progress, completed projects, theses and dissertations. The session will provide a supportive environment for scholarly feedback, interdisciplinary dialogue and networking with scholars from across institutions. Proposal Formats We welcome: Individual papers Panel discussions Poster presentations Creative and multimedia works Workshops and interactive sessions Who Should Submit? Graduate students, faculty, researchers and practitioners from all disciplines are encouraged to submit original work that engages with the conference theme. Proposal Guidelines Proposals should be 300-600 words, depending on disciplinary standards, and address: Title - A concise, descriptive title that engages an interdisciplinary audience. Purpose and Central Question/Problem - The primary aim of the work. Conceptual, Theoretical or Disciplinary Framework - The intellectual foundation of the work. Methods, Materials or Creative Approach - How the work was conducted or developed. Findings, Claims or Scholarly Contribution - The work's intellectual contribution. Interdisciplinary Significance and Broader Impact - The relevance of the work beyond a single discipline. For panels, submit an individual abstract for each paper. How Proposals Are Reviewed All proposals will undergo peer review and will be evaluated based on: Clarity and coherence Scholarly rigor Methodological or interpretive soundness Originality and contribution to knowledge Interdisciplinary engagement and accessibility Relevance to the conference theme Conference Information Nov. 8-10, 2026 The Hotel at the University of Maryland Discounted rates are available for conference attendees. Ready to Contribute? Share your research, scholarship or creative work with an interdisciplinary community exploring new approaches to the challenges of the 21st century. Submit your proposal: graduateschool@bowiestate.edu Transformative Synergies Arts, Business, STEM, Health & Education for a Changing World Bowie State University | The Graduate School

items.fullDescription: Abstract: This panel reexamines life writing in the age of Generative AI, asking who controls the conditions under which individuals narrate their own lives. Submissions reflecting on how AI corporations and Generative AI models are reshaping life writing practices across textual, digital, and visual formats, or on the consequences of such practices for authorship, equity, and cultural power, are especially welcome. Full CFP: Generative AI has fundamentally changed how we think, articulate, and write. However, access to AI is not equitable, and its outputs frequently fail to account for diverse lived experiences and reflect biases. The corporations developing AI models are agents actively reshaping how we perceive, think, interpret, and articulate our identities and experiences. This panel examines what that means for Life Writing - defined broadly to include textual, digital, and visual formats - where individuals reflect, narrativize, and present their lived experiences in public-facing contexts. Submissions engaging the conference theme, "Our Ruling Classes: Culture, Power and Conflict," are especially welcome. As Marcel Danesi (2025) observes, "the study of creativity crosses all disciplinary boundaries", making creativity a particularly productive lens through which to examine the teaching and learning of Italian language and culture. items.fullDescription: India's civilizational ethos is deeply rooted in its multilingual and multicultural fabric, where translation has enabled the circulation of ideas, texts, and knowledge across regions and traditions. Etymologically understood as "carrying across," translation in the 21st century extends beyond linguistic transfer to become a critical and interpretive practice. A. K. Ramanujan, in his writings, draws attention to translation's context-sensitive nature, while G. N. Devy highlights the complex linguistic and cultural histories within which translation operates in India. Seen in this light, translation involves negotiation, re-articulation, and the making of new meanings within specific cultural settings. Practices such as transcreation, adaptation, and interpretation highlight the creative potential of translation. At the same time, the increasing use of machine translation and AI-based tools has introduced another dimension, making translation faster and more accessible, while also raising questions about accuracy and interpretation. In view of these varied contexts, practices, and concerns, this seminar aims to provide a platform for students, teachers, and researchers to reflect on the evolving role of translation in contemporary India across literary, academic, and everyday contexts. It seeks to bring together diverse perspectives on both the challenges and possibilities of translating Indian languages in the present day. items.fullDescription: Pendant la période de l'Indochine française, les premiers vietnamiens sont acheminés en Nouvelle-Calédonie en tant que travailleurs sous-contrat dans les mines de nickel. Cette période marque en parallèle la rébellion très présente des autochtones de l'île - les Kanak - face à la dépossession territoriale des colons français. Le refus de participer à l'industrie minière d'un groupe favorise l'expatriation de l'autre sur l'archipel en pleine ère de la colonisation française dans plusieurs colonies. Le roi tonkinois Ham Nghi, à l'âge de 18 ans, a été placé en exil en Algérie après des années de mouvements de résistance contre la puissance coloniale française. Son expulsion fait écho à celle de la Reine malgache Ranavalona III, qui a eu lieu après l'annexion de Madagascar par la France en 1896. L'ensemble de l'empire français, étendu de l'Indochine à l'Afrique insulaire, est sujet à la déportation dans la plus grande colonie de peuplement. Ce réseau de déportation des colonies liées met en avant la question des outils de domination employés par le système colonial. Malgré les différentes populations colonisées, la stratégie de domination s'applique d'une certaine façon. **** Dans le cadre académique au sein des études francophones et françaises, nous voyons souvent des pistes de spécialisation distinctes, telles que les études européennes, les études caribéennes, et les études postcoloniales francophones. Les cours d'histoire et de littérature offrent également des réflexions particulières selon une région spécifique ainsi qu'une époque donnée. L'objectif de former les futurs chercheurs dans des domaines précis, faute d'études approfondies sur les caractéristiques transcontinentales, risque de faire oublier qu'au coeur de l'histoire de l'un est tissée celle de l'autre. Cette imbrication transnationale et transcommunautaire, inévitable soit-elle, est due à la fois aux déplacements migratoires, à l'exil d'après-guerre, et à la mobilisation de la force de travail par le système capitaliste et colonial. Lorsque l'on met en évidence ce lien intrinsèque entre des événements, on fait émerger un réseau transcolonial qui lie l'Afrique, l'Asie, et/ou l'Europe. Ce réseau nous oblige à réfléchir à l'interconnexion de l'un à l'autre, d'une communauté spécifique à une autre soi-disant éloignée. Dans le contexte du monde d'aujourd'hui, une telle conscience de l'interconnexion des histoires coloniales peut susciter des réflexions : Peut-on vraiment ignorer le combat de l'autre ? Quels seront les enjeux ? Communications à envoyer soit en anglais, soit en français.

items.fullDescription: The sea and marine life are often considered as pillars of cultural heritage, identity, and collective memories in Portugal (Lourenço 2001; Lourenço 2014). From the historical milestones of the sixteenth century transoceanic navigation (Cortesão 1978) to literary production (Avelar 2024), the ocean has shaped the national imagination of Portugal (Tomás 2013). As Antonio Barreto writes: "Heritage is a human creation and the results from history and culture. But there are natural realities that are transformed, through history, culture, and technology into heritage. Such is the case of the sea for the Portuguese" (2019: 15). As a form of heritage, this connection extends to gastronomy and, in a particularly profound way, to the musical sphere (Simões 2013: 45-62; Sardo 2013: 44-64). From fado, with its narratives of longing and loss, to the songs that gave rhythm to the the fishermen's daily work, the Portuguese musical repertoire has functioned as a living archive of human interaction with the environment. However, there is nothing natural or essentialist about this Portuguese relationship with the sea, for it is an imaginary that has been constructed and continously negotiated across historical periods, which also bears the imprint of colonialism (João 2015: 119-147; El-Shawan Castelo-Branco et al 2003: 73-142). More dramatically, the transformations driven by climate change and unsustainable industrial fishing in the twenty-first century threaten not only biodiversity (Ramos-Pereira 2004: 26-43), but also the cultural practices linked to it - a topic that still requires greater attention in schoarly research. In any case, beyond its material and economic dimensions, the sea in Portugal remains a space of imagination and transformation. As evoked in the songs of José Afonso, the sea is not just a site of identity and homecoming, but also a place of alterity and utopia. By singing of the sea, we evoke the possibility of a new era, in which culture and nature meet once again in a shared project of humanity - a vision that also resonates with the notion of the Blue Humanities (Mentz 2023; Oppermann 2019: 443-461). This call seeks to explore the intersection between what we have inherited and what we must protect. Therefore, we invite researchers, artists, and cultural practitioners to reflect on how these environmental changes reshape the meaning of the arts and their role as vehicles of identity and resistance. Papers are welcome on the following topics, amongst others: The sea as a cultural construct in Portuguese music and the arts; Music, critique, and resistance to climate crises in Portugal; Intersections between literature, music, and environmental heritage; Representations of the sea and music in literature and written culture; Music, sound, identity, and the politics of ocean memory; Collective memory, local identities, and soundscapes; The sea in film, the media, and popular culture; Folklore, folk groups, and the preservation of intangible cultural heritage; Coloniality and decoloniality of contemporary maritime identity; Transcultural and postcolonial perspectives on the maritime imaginary; Blue Humanities and music as an environmental archive; Resistance, utopia, and sound activism in the face of climate change; Tourism and heritage preservation of coastal musical cultures; Technology, marine sciences, and music; Ocean ethics, music, and maritime imaginaries; Phenomenology, aesthetics, listening, and maritime experience. Call for Proposals Business English education sits at the intersection of education, professional communication, and global social change. In a world shaped by geopolitical tensions, economic inequalities, technological disruption, and cultural polarization, communication across cultural contexts is both more necessary and more complex than ever. Business English therefore involves more than teaching linguistic skills for the workplace; it also prepares learners to deal with cultural diversity, power structures, and ethical decision-making in international professional contexts. Effective professional communication today requires not only exchanging information but also negotiating meaning, building trust, and collaborating across cultures and perspectives. Business English courses support university students, vocational learners, and professionals in developing communicative competence, intercultural awareness, and confidence in multilingual workplaces. In many contexts, this work involves collaboration with corporate partners and engagement with current workplace practices, while also encouraging critical reflection on whose voices are heard in professional communication. The role of the business English educator is therefore to help learners bridge multiple gaps: between education and professional practice, between various cultures, and between local experiences and global systems. In a fragmented and rapidly changing world, business English education can help create spaces for inclusive, responsible, and effective professional communication. This year's conference invites contributions that explore how business English education can respond to these challenges and build the bridges needed for meaningful intercultural understanding. items.fullDescription: Call for Chapters Rhetoric and Communication. Interdisciplinary Studies in the Humanities The intersection of Rhetoric and Communication continues to attract the interest of many scholars, particularly within the fields of the Humanities and Social Sciences. The scope of analysis is wide-ranging, encompassing literature and culture, language studies and advertising, communication studies and politics, among other domains. In this Volume, we aim to bring together a set of studies that focus directly on topics shared by Rhetoric and Communication, from Classical Antiquity to the present, from an interdisciplinary perspective. Scholarly contributions across the Humanities will enhance our understanding of the influence of rhetoric and communication on society, taking into account, on the one hand, there is a vast legacy that merits further study and, on the other, new forms of communication require us to reassess the impact of the rhetorical art. This Volume welcomes contributions of a theoretical or empirical nature, including case studies, from within the field of the Humanities. Possible topics include: · Rhetorical and communication theory applied to discourse; · Treatises on rhetoric and communication; · The presence of rhetorical genres in contemporary forms of communication; · Argumentation techniques and persuasion in literary texts, the media, advertising, or other narrative forms; · The contemporary relevance of teaching rhetoric and communication; · The contemporary application of classical rhetoric in the media; · Rhetoric in political discourse and in literary composition; · Philosophical perspectives on rhetoric and communication; · The role of the audience and the addressee in rhetorical theory and in the communicative process; · Representations of rhetoric and communication in the Arts. items.fullDescription: The Centre for Research on Language and Culture Contact invites you to submit an abstract for Resisting Abandonment: Language, Culture, and Ecology, an interdisciplinary conference that will explore the ways in which ecology intersects with language contact, cultural transformation, and pedagogical practice. Conference Dates: October 15-16, 2026 Location: Glendon College -York University (Toronto, Canada) Keynote Speaker: Daniel Frost, Professor of Spanish and of Latin American, Latinx, and Caribbean Studies, College of the Holy Cross Abstracts Due: June 15, 2026 - - - - - - - - - - - - - Le Centre de recherche sur le contact des langues et des cultures vous invite à soumettre un résumé pour Résister à l'abandon : langue, culture et écologie, un colloque interdisciplinaire qui explorera les liens entre l'écologie, le contact linguistique, la transformation culturelle et les pratiques pédagogiques. Dates du colloque : 15-16 octobre 2026 Lieu : Collège universitaire Glendon - Université York (Toronto, Canada) Conférencier principal : Daniel Frost, professeur d'espagnol et d'études latino-américaines, latinx et caribéennes, College of the Holy Cross Date limite de soumission des résumés : 15 juin 2026 - - - - - - - - - - - - - International Conference Resisting Abandonment: Language, Culture, and Ecology Centre for Research on Language and Culture Contact Glendon College, York University (Toronto, Canada) October 15-16, 2026 The Centre for Research on Language and Culture Contact invites you to an interdisciplinary conference that will explore the ways in which ecology intersects with language contact, cultural transformation, and pedagogical practice. Resisting Abandonment is inspired by Sunaura Taylor's groundbreaking book Disabled Ecologies: Lessons from a Wounded Desert (2024), which challenges dominant environmental narratives by centring disability, care, and interdependence. The conference aims to build on Taylor's theorization of abandonment - material and ideological - which manifests in polluted landscapes, dispossessed communities, endangered languages, and marginalized bodies. Ecological degradation and linguistic erosion often unfold together, shaped by colonialism, extractivism, migration, and neoliberal restructuring. In Ecolinguistics: Language, Ecology, and the Stories We Live By (2020), Arran Stibbe articulates the ways in which ecolinguistic inquiry - including language-contact studies - reveals how knowledges of living sustainably in the local environment are embedded in endangered languages and are vulnerable to the global spread of dominant languages. Threats to linguistic diversity can be correlated to diminished biodiversity. Resisting Abandonment will foreground the idea that languages, like ecosystems, are sites of relationality and care. When communities are displaced by climate crises, economic dispossession, or other factors, their linguistic practices shift, hybridize, or face erasure. Yet contact zones also generate creative survivance: new vernaculars, embodied knowledges, and solidarities across difference. The conference convenes scholars, educators, translators, artists, and community advocates to examine how practices of naming, storytelling, teaching, and translating can resist ecological, linguistic, and cultural abandonment. How do metaphors of purity and contamination shape both environmental and linguistic policy? What can disability justice teach us about sustaining multilingual ecologies of access? How might translation function as a form of environmental care work? Participants will explore the ethical and political stakes of attending to fragile ecologies - human and more-than-human - without reproducing narratives of loss that justify further neglect. Resisting Abandonment invites collective reflection on care as method, contact as creativity, and interdependence as a framework for ecological and linguistic futures. Examples of subtopics by discipline: Cultural Studies : analyzing representations of ecological and linguistic wastelands - including their recuperation and adaptation - in media and literature of former and current power sites and/or in post/neocolonial texts. Linguistics : examining how ecological loss accelerates language endangerment or, conversely, how language erosion facilitates ecological loss; reflecting on whether documentation practices themselves risk reproducing extractive models Sociolinguistics : studies of language contact in climate-displaced communities; examining codeswitching as ecological adaptation Translation Studies : translating environmental knowledge across Indigenous and minoritized languages without epistemic extraction Pedagogy : designing care-centred, place-based curricula that link environmental justice with multilingual education Communication Studies : analyzing how environmental crises and linguistic marginalization are framed across media, policy discourse, and digital platforms; probing how choice of language used in the media influences how communities think about ecological issues and/or manufactures consent Second-Language Teaching : incorporating local ecological narratives into L2 classrooms to foster environmental and intercultural care Minority-Language Advocacy : examining how environmental policy, urban planning, and disaster response frequently neglect linguistic accessibility, thereby compounding abandonment or proposing strategies for integrating language justice into climate-resilience planning Those interested in contributing to the conference with a 20-minute paper should send a title, 200-word abstract, and short biography to crlcc@glendon.yorku.ca by June 15, 2026. Colloque international Résister à l'abandon: langue, culture et écologie Centre de recherche sur le contact des langues et des cultures Collège universitaire Glendon, Université York (Toronto, Canada) 15 et 16 octobre 2026 Le Centre de recherche sur le contact des langues et des cultures vous invite à un colloque interdisciplinaire qui explorera les manières dont l'écologie interagit avec le contact entre les langues, avec les transformations culturelles et avec les pratiques pédagogiques. Résister à l'abandon s'inspire de l'ouvrage marquant de Sunaura Taylor, Disabled Ecologies: Lessons from a Wounded Desert (2024), qui remet en question les récits environnementaux dominants à la lumière du handicap, du respect et de l'interdépendance. Le colloque vise à approfondir la théorisation de l'abandon, à la fois matériel et idéologique, proposée par Taylor, qui se manifeste dans des paysages pollués, des communautés dépossédées, des langues en voie de disparition et des corps marginalisés. La dégradation écologique et l'érosion linguistique évoluent souvent conjointement, façonnées par le colonialisme, l'extractivisme, les migrations et les restructurations néolibérales. Dans Ecolinguistics: Language, Ecology, and the Stories We Live By (2020), Arran Stibbe met en lumière la manière dont les approches écolinguistiques, y compris les études sur le contact entre les langues, permettent de mieux comprendre les liens entre langue et environnement. Les menaces qui pèsent sur la diversité linguistique peuvent ainsi être reliées à l'appauvrissement de la biodiversité. Résister à l'abandon mettra en avant l'idée que les langues, à l'instar des écosystèmes, constituent des espaces de relation et de respect. Lorsque des communautés sont déplacées par des crises climatiques, la dépossession économique ou d'autres facteurs, leurs pratiques linguistiques se transforment, s'hybrident ou risquent de disparaître. Pourtant, les zones de contact engendrent également des formes créatives de survie: de nouveaux vernaculaires, des savoirs incarnés et des solidarités au-delà des différences. Le colloque réunit des chercheur·e·s, enseignant·e·s, traducteurs/trices, artistes et militant·e·s communautaires afin d'examiner comment les pratiques de nomination, de narration, d'enseignement et de traduction peuvent résister à l'abandon écologique, linguistique et culturel. Comment les métaphores de pureté et de contamination influencent-elles les politiques environnementales et linguistiques? Que peut nous apprendre la justice du handicap sur le maintien d'écologies multilingues accessibles? De quelle manière la traduction peut-elle fonctionner comme une forme de soin environnemental? Les participant·e·s réfléchiront aux enjeux éthiques et politiques liés à l'attention portée aux écologies fragiles, humaines et plus qu'humaines, sans reproduire des récits de perte qui justifient davantage de négligence. Résister à l'abandon invite à une réflexion collective sur le respect en tant que méthode, sur le contact comme créativité et sur l'interdépendance comme cadre pour penser les futurs écologiques et linguistiques. Exemples de sous-thèmes par discipline : Études culturelles : analyser les représentations des déserts écologiques et linguistiques, y compris leur récupération et leur adaptation, dans les médias et la littérature issus de centres de pouvoir, anciens ou actuels, et/ou dans des textes post/néocoloniaux Linguistique : examiner comment la perte écologique accélère la disparition des langues ou, inversement, comment l'érosion linguistique facilite la perte écologique; réfléchir à la possibilité que les pratiques de documentation elles-mêmes reproduisent des modèles extractivistes Sociolinguistique : étudier le contact entre les langues dans des communautés déplacées par les changements climatiques; analyser l'alternance codique comme forme d'adaptation écologique Traductologie : traduire les connaissances environnementales dans les langues autochtones et minoritaires sans extraction épistémique Pédagogie et didactique : concevoir des programmes axés sur les soins et ancrés dans le territoire, qui associent la justice environnementale à l'éducation multilingue Études en communication : analyser la manière dont les crises environnementales et la marginalisation linguistique sont représentées dans les médias, les discours politiques et les plateformes numériques; examiner comment les choix linguistiques dans les médias influencent la manière dont les communautés pensent les enjeux écologiques et contribuent à fabriquer le consentement Enseignement d'une langue seconde : intégrer des récits écologiques locaux dans les cours de langue seconde afin de promouvoir le respect de l'environnement et l'ouverture interculturelle Promotion des langues minoritaires : examiner comment les politiques environnementales, l'urbanisme et les interventions en cas de catastrophe négligent souvent l'accessibilité linguistique, ce qui accentue l'abandon de ces communautés, ou proposer des stratégies visant à intégrer la justice linguistique dans la planification de la résilience climatique Si vous souhaitez contribuer au colloque avec une communication de 20 minutes, veuillez envoyer un titre, un résumé de 200 mots et une courte biographie à crlcc@glendon.yorku.ca avant le 15 juin 2026. items.fullDescription: Transatlantic Connections and the 'Special Relationship[s]': BAAS Postgraduate Symposium, 2026 V&A East Storehouse, London 9th November In 1946, Winston Churchill declared the need for a "special relationship between the British Commonwealth and Empire and the United States" in order to maintain world diplomacy, citing our shared language and cultural values as connecting the two countries. Although this 'special relationship' has continually been called into question by scholars, there is undoubtedly a channel of cultural and political exchange between the US and the UK, as well as with other countries, which has become even more urgent for discussion in recent years. The 2026 BAAS Postgraduate Symposium invites proposals from postgraduate researchers at all levels and across all disciplines on the topic of Transatlantic Connections and the 'Special Relationship[s]'. By using the term 'Special Relationship[s]', we intend to explore the relationship between not only the US and the UK, but also between the US and other countries. We invite panels and individual papers on this theme and encourage you to interpret it as broadly as you wish, including any aspect of the US's transnational cultural, political and literary connections, influences or contrasts. We welcome contributions from all realms of American Studies, including, but not limited to: literature and film studies, postcolonial and decolonial analysis, science and visual culture, and urban and environmental history. As this year's symposium will be held at V&A East Storehouse, the site of the David Bowie Archive, we are particularly keen on hearing from scholars exploring the etymologically and culturally rich prefix of the term 'Transatlantic' itself. This one-day symposium will involve not only academic panel discussions, but other activities such as a career development session, an introduction to the archives at the Victoria and Albert Museum, and a keynote address by Professor Mark Ford. The intention is to foster a strong postgraduate community in American Studies and to learn from both our peers and from leaders in our field. The symposium will be catered, hosted primarily in-person at V&A East Storehouse, but with a digital attendance option for those only able to join online. There will be time in the day to explore V&A East Storehouse and the David Bowie Centre. V&A East Storehouse is a working museum store with a rich archive for students to use in their research. The building is designed to allow visitors to get closer to objects held in the V&A collections and to the work of the museum itself. We welcome the submission of individual papers as well as proposals for complete panels of three researchers. Applications from groups of three or four researchers for roundtable discussions are also welcome. For panel and roundtable proposals, please also include a statement of up to 200 words on the aims of the collective submission, alongside the individual papers. Papers should be around 15-20 minutes long , and roundtables will consist of five-minute introductions by each researcher followed by 45 minutes of discussion. Interdisciplinary paper, panel and roundtable proposals are encouraged. Suggested paper and roundtable topics include, but are not limited to: - Case studies or broader comparisons between literary texts from the US and other nations - Case studies or broader comparisons between films from the US and other nations - Comparative political or historical analyses concerning the US and other nations - Comparative economic, scientific or environmental analyses concerning the US and other nations. Although the symposium will centre on 'Transatlantic Connections', we welcome proposals making any transnational comparisons rooted in American Studies. We especially encourage researchers from across Europe and beyond to submit and attend, as part of ongoing efforts to expand the EAAS community of postgraduates. We want to make this symposium as accessible as possible; we will be working to ensure a relaxed academic environment and we encourage anyone attending to email us with any access needs. Bursaries will be available from BAAS on a limited basis for students requiring financial support for attendance. The deadline for submissions is? 15th September 2026 .?Please send proposals including a title, an abstract of no more than? 250 words ?and?a short biography of no more than 200 words ?to Claire Watt at?claire.watt@baas.ac.uk. If you have any questions about the symposium, big or small, please get in touch and we will be happy to help. We look forward to hearing from you!

items.fullDescription: When we trace the genealogy of crisis, it can seem as if we've always been surrounded by catastrophe. Different factions of the ruling class tell us that we need to be prepared, but also that preparation may be fruitless. Crises shift and expand, strengthening their hold on us through their very instability. The state of emergency, after all, "is not the exception but the rule," as Walter Benjamin theorized. It is not a single event but what Lauren Berlant called a norm "embedded" in the everyday. In the zones of crisis and in daily life, the emergency overwhelms the senses, requiring constant self-governance and limiting our political imagination. The urgent threat of climate change, though often disavowed, is at the center of today's general atmosphere of crisis. Walls hold back displaced populations and rising seas. Earth systems sustain lasting damage. Species are devastated. And with apocalyptic alacrity, capitalist-imperialist competition crosses terrains that were once uninviting and hostile, from deserts to the polar regions and outer space. So far, discourses of risk and emergency have mostly been a boon for the racist right and anti-democratic technocrats, rather than contributing to a genuine project of planetary stewardship. The quest for "energy sovereignty" has unleashed a wave of extractive interventions in the Global South amid the collapse of the postwar international order, creating new sacrifice zones and colonial resource frontiers. Amid widespread doubts about electoral institutions' ability to deliver systemic transformation, some environmentalists have even embraced climate doomerism or the technosolutionism of geoengineering. We see how climate crisis is increasingly governed through biopolitical management, securitized borders, and technocratic forms of environmental control-and how the emergency becomes yet another opportunity for further administration. Crisis discourse often privileges spectacular catastrophe while obscuring the slow, uneven, and racialized forms of ecological violence embedded in everyday life. Unlike the "fevered immediacy that governs the society of the catastrophe-as-spectacle," as Rob Nixon writes, unspectacular "slow violence" is dispersed over time. With the sirens blaring, it is easy to lose sight of the material impacts of the ideology of crisis across time and space. We can also miss the ways in which the permanent emergency warps our cultural production and social relations, concealing the most pressing contradictions of capitalism today. How might we map the cartography of crisis? In doing so, might we open space for alternative ways of thinking and living within and against crisis? How do we hold crisis at bay long enough to bring about a "real state of emergency," as Benjamin says is our task? Jason W. Moore (Binghamton) and Gökçe Günel (Rice) will deliver keynote addresses at the conference, which will also feature a curated program of poetry readings and film screenings. In Case of Emergency is organized by Aditi Kini, Tadhg Larabee, Ernest Lee, and Yolian Ogbu in collaboration with the Chicago Center for Contemporary Theory, and with support from the Committee on Environment, Geography, and Urbanization. To apply, submit an abstract (max. 300 words) and a CV via this Google form by June 30, 2026: https://forms.gle/Fj4r9oAk5r8b6Q5K6 We want to investigate how crisis is produced, circulated, and inhabited across domains, including climate, culture, political economy, media, and governance. Through this cartography of crisis, we hope to understand how we might countermap and counteract this state of ecological and social emergency. We invite proposals from graduate students in the humanities and social sciences, as well as artists, writers, and other practitioners. Our goal is to create space for imagination and speculation with people of varied backgrounds, interests, and praxes. We welcome interdisciplinary scholarship and cultural criticism attentive to the cultural, aesthetic, historical, and political dimensions of crisis. We imagine submissions might discuss: Technosolutionism and the dilemmas of growth Speculation, commodities, and disaster capitalism Fossil life as economy and desire Green neoliberalism as a political and cultural form Enclosure and destruction of the commons: water, forests, air and more Hydrocolonialism, oceanic crisis, and blue humanities Border ecologies, displacement, and the production of space State-making, world-making, and the remaking of political, social and ecological orders Toxic temporalities, slow violence, and "post"-colonial precarity Apocalypse and new worlds in literature and culture Climate pessimisms and the politics of fear and hope in crisis Resistance, strikes, and land back: movements and solidarity Community, care, and affective ecologies of crisis Participants without access to institutional funding will have the opportunity to request travel support, though we cannot guarantee it. Questions for the organizers can be sent to ccct@uchicago.edu.

items.fullDescription: Engaging with PAMLA's 2026 theme, "Our Ruling Classes: Culture, Power, Conflict," this panel asks: How do esoteric ecological imaginaries reinforce, negotiate, or resist ruling ideologies? How have spiritualized visions of nature shaped elite cultural production, countercultural movements, or alternative political communities? What conflicts emerge when esoteric environmental ethics confront institutional religion, scientific rationalism, or capitalist extraction? Topics of interest include, but are not limited to, literary representations of enchanted ecologies, spiritual ecologies in travel writing or poetic form, occult environmental metaphysics, and the role of esoteric belief in shaping ecological imaginaries. We welcome historically grounded and theoretically informed approaches to literature, art, travel writing, popular culture, and critical theory. Topics may include ecospirituality, occult environmentalism, esoteric dimensions of deep ecology, and aesthetic practices that envision enchanted or spiritually animated landscapes as sites of cultural struggle and renewal. To submit a paper and present, you must become a PAMLA member by paying the member fee and the conference fee. items.fullDescription: Please consider submitting to the ACLA seminar titled "South-South Literary Relations and the Remaking of World Literature" by September 21, 2026 . You can submit your abstracts here: https://www.acla.org/cfp/70fe7418-c14a-468d-be1d-809e878f2e00/submit-paper/46d872df-9512-49a7-89f7-8bc710370693 Abstract from the ACLA CFP: Since the rise of World Literature as a major field of inquiry, discussions of literary circulation have often privileged routes that pass through metropolitan centers, emphasizing translation into dominant European languages, global publishing networks, and institutions located in the Global North. Yet literary works have long traveled through alternative circuits that connect regions of the Global South directly, producing histories of exchange that challenge center-periphery models of cultural transmission. This seminar invites papers that examine literary relationships among Africa, Asia, Latin America, the Caribbean, SWANA, Oceania, and other locations within the Global South. Such relationships may emerge through translation, political solidarity, migration, anti-colonial movements, publishing networks, educational institutions, shared aesthetic projects, or indirect forms of influence. They may also involve moments in which Northern institutions, languages, or markets facilitate, mediate, redirect, or constrain South-South encounters, raising questions about whether these exchanges can ever be understood as entirely autonomous. Rather than treating the Global South as a unified category, the seminar seeks to explore its internal heterogeneity, asymmetries of power, and competing visions of solidarity. How do texts travel between Southern contexts? What historical, linguistic, and political conditions make these encounters possible? What role do translators, publishers, periodicals, archives, and digital media play in creating or sustaining South-South literary networks? How might these circulations reshape concepts such as influence, comparison, translation, reception, or worldliness? We especially welcome papers that interrogate the implications of South-South literary exchange for the study of World Literature itself. If literary circulation is not exclusively organized through Northern centers, what alternative maps of World Literature become visible? Can South-South networks offer different ways of imagining literary value, canon formation, and global comparison? By foregrounding overlooked routes of circulation and exchange, this seminar aims to reconsider how World Literature is conceptualized and to illuminate the multiple worlds through which literature moves. Possible topics include, but are not limited to: South-South translation; comparative studies across the Global South; Cold War and Non-Aligned literary networks; postcolonial and decolonial approaches; migration and diaspora; publishing and periodical cultures; digital literary circulation; transregional modernisms; indigenous and vernacular exchanges; reception studies; archives of literary solidarity; and new theoretical approaches to World Literature.

items.fullDescription: Abstract This seminar proposes to examine Italian and Italian American food studies through the comparative frameworks of transnational circulation, intermedial representation, and cultural translation. Rather than approaching food as a stable marker of heritage or authenticity, the seminar treats it as a mobile signifying practice through which texts, images, commodities, and affects travel across linguistic, national, and medial boundaries. Food thus becomes a privileged comparative object: it links literature to film, advertising to visual culture, and national discourse to diasporic rearticulation. The seminar invites papers that explore how Italian and Italian American food cultures are narrated, aestheticized, commodified, and contested across literary, cinematic, televisual, and digital forms. Of particular interest are projects that place works, archives, or media formations in relation to one another in order to theorize how "Italian" food is translated across contexts and how those translations produce asymmetries of value, legitimacy, and cultural capital. Such an approach underscores a central concern of comparative literature: the movement of forms, meanings, and imaginaries across borders, alongside the transformations that occur in passage. Theoretically, the seminar welcomes contributions grounded in food studies, diaspora studies, affect theory, queer theory, translation studies, media theory, postcolonial critique, and the study of racial capitalism. Food may be read here not only as representation, but also as material practice and epistemic structure: a medium through which embodiment, labor, memory, desire, and power become legible. This framing allows participants to ask how culinary discourse organizes identity and difference, how commensality produces or unsettles forms of belonging, and how domestic, commercial, and national narratives intersect in the production of italianità. The seminar is especially interested in comparative work on themes such as authenticity and simulacra; migration and coloniality; domestic labor and social reproduction; gastronomy and class distinction; queer kinship and alternative temporalities; and the branding of "Made in Italy" in global consumer culture. Papers may address novels, memoirs, cinema, television, cookbooks, food writing, advertisements, social media, or other cultural texts. By bringing Italian and Italian American materials into sustained dialogue, the seminar seeks to show how food serves as a crucial analytic for comparative literary study: one that illuminates mediation, circulation, translation, and the uneven politics of cultural value in a globalized world.

items.fullDescription: This ACLA seminar asks what it means to teach the "world" in fields such as world cinema, world literature, comparative literature, and global media studies. Courses organized around the world often promise breadth, diversity, and cross-cultural understanding, but they also face practical and conceptual problems. What counts as the world? How does the nation appear in "world" courses? How do syllabi balance coverage, depth, translation, historical context, aesthetics, and political urgency? How do institutional expectations and restrictions mold the student imagination of the "world"? How does the positionality of the instructor presuppose, structure, or influence the "world" classroom? The seminar invites papers on the pedagogy of world cinema, media, literature, and related fields. We welcome reflections on syllabus design, classroom practice, study abroad programs, canonicity, national, regional, and transnational frameworks, diaspora, migration, colonial and postcolonial histories, language, accessibility, and the politics of curation. Participants might address how a single course constructs the world, how students respond to unfamiliar forms and contexts, how films or texts travel across classrooms, or how teaching the world changes across institutional locations. Through the discussions generated by this seminar, we hope to gather strategies for reimagining "world" courses in film, literature, and new media classrooms. Therefore, this seminar is especially interested in approaches that treat pedagogy as a site of theory. How do teaching practices revise our understanding of the world itself? What models of the world do our classrooms reproduce, and what alternative worlds might they make possible? We welcome both theoretical reflections and concrete case studies, including discussions of specific courses, syllabi, assignments, classroom practices, films, texts, or teaching contexts. items.excerpt: Emotions continue to attract critical attention across disciplines. Over the past three decades, emotion theory has provided a multidisciplinary lens for understanding literary and cult...
items.fullDescription: Emotions continue to attract critical attention across disciplines. Scholars have noted the growing prominence of emotion in media, politics, and internet culture, which some describe as an "emotionalization" of social life (Yanacek 2026). Over the past three decades, emotion theory has provided a multidisciplinary lens for understanding literary and cultural texts, phenomena, and movements. Brian Massumi's distinction holds that emotion is socially coded and contingent on language, whereas affect is a pre-linguistic, asignifying intensity that exceeds discourse's capacity to fully capture it (1995). Sara Ahmed reframes emotion as social and relational rather than private, arguing that emotions "stick" to bodies and objects through repeated circulation, accumulating or losing affective value in the process (2004). Historians such as Barbara Rosenwein instead approach emotion diachronically, investigating the sanctioned "emotional communities" of different historical periods and how their norms of feeling and expression changed over time (2006). These frameworks are not fully reconcilable. For example, Massumi's model of pre-personal intensity has been challenged by critics such as Ruth Leys (2011), who question whether a truly pre-social affect is theoretically or empirically defensible. This tension among circulation, historicization, and the limit of pre-linguistic feeling remains a live and generative debate in the field. Game studies extend this inquiry into interactive media, asking scholars to account for procedure, system, and player agency alongside representation when studying emotion in play and design. Meanwhile, recent advances in facial recognition and artificial intelligence have pushed machines "from analytical processors to emotionally perceptive entities," if not to emotional entities themselves (Slimani 2026). These approaches resist treating emotion as ahistorical, private, or apolitical. Studying feeling as a legitimate, theorizable object reveals how power operates through affect, opens texts to modes of engagement beyond decoding, and invites us to reconsider the boundaries of the human, including where those boundaries fall in relation to nonhuman and machine forms of feeling. This panel invites papers that develop, test, or complicate existing theories of affect and emotion through close case studies, rather than merely applying them. We welcome submissions on any literary or cultural form, including but not limited to novels, poetry, drama, film, and video games, from any historical period and geographical region. This panel will be held online. Please go to https://www.acla.org/seminars, log into your ACLA account, find the panel, and submit your paper proposal by clicking the submit button.

items.fullDescription: Papers with a specifically comparative focus on the sins of reading (Peccata Lectionis) can examine the topic of the seminar from a theoretical, methodological and thematic perspective. If we speak about the event of reading in a general sense, misreading as an interpretative act should not necessarily be defined as a sin or even as a mistake. At least, this cannot be done as clearly as in a legal, ethical or psychological discourse about sin or a mistake in the case of a Mozart overture played out of tune. What then is the sin of reading? From a theoretical point of view, it may well be defined as a complement to "the virtue of reading" (Virtus Lectionis, Ambrus 2026). All this creates a connection between the literary canon and canonisation known from the Christian religious tradition, and perhaps the sin of reading lies in non-canonical interpretation. Also, literary critics as professional readers can commit one of the sins of reading when losing their credibility with lay people watching them. However, the most radical theoretical and methodological problem stems from language itself. If we give credit to Nietzsche's philosophical claims on language adopted from Gustav Gerber, we must also consider language itself and hence literature as an accumulation of errors, in accordance with Paul Ricoeur's theory of metaphor, identifying the origin of tropes as linguistic errors. The professional reading of literature, which is considered as a set of mistakes, is already lying when it discusses its subject not as rhetorical errors, but as aesthetic quality. When we study the literary works of different cultures and periods and think about the sins related to reading, we can come to a similar conclusion. The seminar welcomes any comparative and even interdisciplinary paper that wants to take into account the above problems of reading, primarily in association with the Judeo-Christian tradition and sin understood according to Western philosophical concepts. From a literary point of view, special attention may be paid to the works of Aristophanes, Dante, Cervantes, Laurence Sterne, E. T. A. Hoffmann, Henry James, Marcel Proust, Virginia Woolf, James Joyce, Jorge Luis Borges or Paul Auster, and from a religious point of view, to the works of Philo of Alexandria, the Kabbalist thinkers, Origen, Saint Augustine, Hugh of Saint Victor, Ticonius, Rudolf Bultmann, Northrop Frye, Gershom Scholem, and David Tracy.
