items.fullDescription: This seminar examines performance as a multilayered concept that is continually reshaped through travel and other mobilities. Performance, in this context, can be understood in its broadest sense as a dynamic practice through which identities, relationships, meanings, and experiences are negotiated and transformed. By bringing performance and mobilities into conversation as mutually illuminating frameworks, the seminar seeks to explore how their intersection creates new critical possibilities. Thinking about performance vis-à-vis mobilities draws attention to the varied forms through which these practices take shape and acquire meaning. For instance, Tim Edensor applies the "metaphor of performance" to tourism, examining how tourist practices may be "regulated, directed and choreographed" while also allowing for "improvisation and contestation" (59). The connection between performance and mobilities also foregrounds how performed identities mediate access to movement across different spaces. Jeanne Baret's participation in Louis Antoine de Bougainville's expedition in the eighteenth century while disguised as "Jean," for example, demonstrates how gender performance became a condition of mobility, as women "donned masculine garb when they wished to enter where women otherwise dared not tread" (Schiebinger 24). Travelling performances further demonstrate how mobility is not merely a context for these practices but can become part of the performative process itself. Little Amal, a giant puppet representing a young Syrian refugee girl and part of the art project The Walk, exemplifies this relationship by transforming her journey across cities and borders into an embodied encounter with displacement. This seminar invites further inquiry into the expansive relationship between performance and mobilities, exploring the many ways their intersection can be approached and rethought across historical periods, cultural contexts, literary genres, and modes of expression. Possible topics include (but are not limited to): Performances of identity (gender, race, nationality, class, caste, etc.). Tourism and the performance of authenticity. Migration, displacement, and belonging. Travelling theatre and other itinerant performances. Travel, empire, and performances of knowledge and authority. Religious performances, rituals, and sacred journeys. Social media and curated performances of travel. Writing, documenting, and archiving travel as performance. Travelling figures and cultural encounters. The travelling gaze: voyeurism, surveillance, and spectatorship. Museums, exhibitions, and the mobility of objects. Abstracts must be submitted through the ACLA portal by September 22, 2026. If you have any questions about this seminar, please feel free to contact us: tarafder.rini@gmail.com & achatt5@uwo.ca

items.excerpt: Visualization and imagination have long been recognized as vital to the act of reading. While Russian Formalist Viktor Shklovsky may have denounced the maxim "Art is thinking in images" in his seminal essay "Art as Device" (1917), in favor of strategies of defamiliarization, mental images and imagery are some of the most important ways we engage with a te...
items.fullDescription: Visualization and imagination have long been recognized as vital to the act of reading. While Russian Formalist Viktor Shklovsky may have denounced the maxim "Art is thinking in images" in his seminal essay "Art as Device" (1917), in favor of strategies of defamiliarization, mental images and imagery are some of the most important ways we engage with a text. In Dreaming by the Book , Elaine Scarry describes the function of poetry and novels as "instructions for mental composition" (244). That is, a text encourages readers to fill in the blanks; to reconstruct for themselves certain sensations, emotions, etc. These blanks, according to Wolfgang Iser in The Implied Reader , require readers to draw upon imagination, whereby meaning is created. Ultimately, literature encourages us to envision realities and modalities outside of our own. It is for this reason that reading fiction is considered to be an exercise in empathy--which Marco Caracciolo and Karin Kukkonen conceptualize to be a form of feeling with; of "imagining what we take him or her to be experiencing at a given moment" ( With Bodies: Narrative Theory and Embodied Cognition , 76). This seminar invites papers which attend to the function of visualization, imagination, and/or empathy in reading. In particular, participants are asked to consider how texts across a variety of genres, languages, time periods, cultural contexts, and subject positions, encourage similar or convergent ways of visualization, imagination, and empathy. Can we say reading is "thinking in images"? To what degree do texts encourage the generation of mental imagery and does this necessarily lead us to empathize? How does reading differ phenomenologically from engagement with other arts and mediums? What are the implications of cultivating an embodied and empathetic reading experience, particularly in an era of increasing polarization and automatization? How do certain texts reflect historical and cultural variations in bodily experience? We welcome interdisciplinary approaches drawing from affect theory, narratology, reader-response theory, phenomenology, psychoanalysis, cognitive literary studies, and other related fields. Possible topics may include, but are not limited to: Theories of mind (ToM) and cognitive approaches to reading; embodied models of reading. The impact of genre and form(at): fiction vs. non-fiction, literary vs. genre fiction, nonstandard/"non-literary" texts. Differences across bodies: gender, race, ethnicity, nationality, religion, and/or ability of readers, authors, narrators, and/or characters. Reading in translation or in different languages and effects on the ways we visualize, imagine, and empathize. Theories of imagination, literary imagination, and limits to imagination in reading. Narratological inquiries; impact of perspective and focalization impact on how we visualize and empathize. Reading in the age of Artificial Intelligence. How do AI/LLMs read and how do we read works produced by them?

items.fullDescription: In the introduction to the Fourth Edition of The Norton Anthology of African American Literature, Henry Louis Gates Jr. and Valerie Smith emphasize the imitativeness of literature-Black literature, specifically. To them, literature begets newer literature. At the same time, readers have traced formal patterns of repetition and imitation in Black literature across centuries, dating back to the antebellum. For instance, "Flight to Canada" by Ishmael Reed and "Kindred" by Octavia Butler; Harriet Tubman's "Incidents in the Life of a Slave Girl" and Colson Whitehead's The Underground Railroad, published almost two centuries after Incidents; Mark Twain's Huckleberry Finn and Percival Everette's 2024 "James." These examples reinforce the notion that newer Black literature echoes, borrows, and imitates seminal literatures. This seminar thus seeks to investigate how Black literary and cultural productions have imitated other, earlier literary productions, even across genres and geographical boundaries-like what the editors of the anthology The Negro Caravan (1944) called "a sort of literary inbreeding which causes Negro writers to be influenced by other Negroes…" Even Kwame Anthony Appiah recently aver that "the history of art is the history of people borrowing and adapting techniques and tropes from earlier works." We seek papers that-using fictional and non-fictional Black writings and art-connect the past to the present-papers that explore "imitation," "influence," and "intertextuality" as central to Black literature and Black arts. Guiding questions to consider include, but are not limited to: What literary traditions have endured across generations, and how have they survived? What forms of continuity exist across Black literary history-Plantation to post-bellum literary and cultural productions, Africa to the Diaspora, across centuries, etc.? How do Black writers create new meanings from older texts? What role does memory play in Black literary traditions? How do contemporary writers preserve or challenge earlier literary traditions? How does Black literature reinvent its own past? What histories continue to shape Black literary expression? How do questions of race, identity, and freedom evolve across Black literary history? What earlier genres continue to influence Black literature today? How does Black literature balance tradition and innovation? What can earlier Black literature teach us about contemporary Black writing? items.fullDescription: This seminar proposes to approach William S. Burroughs not simply as a subject of study, but as a problem. We invite provocative papers grounded in comparative methodologies and attentive to less-travelled texts, episodes, affiliations, and cultural encounters. Rather than asking what Burroughs "was," we want to ask what his work does-and to pause over the categories through which we have learned to understand his oeuvre, asking what they illuminate and, perhaps more importantly, what they conceal. What notions of authorship, originality, literary value, sexuality, politics, nationality, identity, language, media, knowledge, or artistic production did Burroughs put under pressure? What happens when his writing is read alongside figures, traditions, media, or intellectual histories with which it is not usually associated? Can Burroughs's experiments still unsettle us? And what do we make of his political views today? We are interested in archival work, but not simply in the recovery of origins or the reconstruction of authorial intention. Archives can instead be approached as contested sites of selection, mediation, myth-making, and afterlife. We are equally interested in familiar Burroughsian techniques-cut-up, collage, montage, sampling, recording-when they are placed in unexpected comparative contexts. What do these techniques actually do? How have they travelled beyond Burroughs? How are they being used today, and by whom? We also welcome papers willing to be unfriendly to their subject. Is Burroughs overrated? Is he politically embarrassing, historically compromised, or aesthetically exhausted? Is he already "cancelled"-or has cancellation itself become another way of making cultural icons safe? Can Burroughs be restored, and if so, to what? Or is he damaged beyond repair? What might we gain by taking seriously the possibility that some of his work should be rejected rather than rescued? Possible approaches include, but are not limited to: Burroughs and writers, artists, or intellectual traditions with which he is rarely compared Burroughs and competing theories of authorship, originality, and literary value Archives, censorship, canonization, and the production of literary authority Burroughs and the politics of race, gender, sexuality, class, empire, and nationality Burroughs's relationship to religion, esotericism, anthropology, science, medicine, and alternative forms of knowledge Literary and non-literary media: sound, film, photography, visual art, performance, television, and digital culture Adaptation, appropriation, influence, imitation, and misreading The contemporary uses and abuses of Burroughs Critical reception, including hostile, skeptical, and revisionist readings We especially welcome proposals that are comparative in more than name: papers that put Burroughs into genuine friction with another author, tradition, medium, language, archive, or conceptual framework. We are less interested in proving that Burroughs anticipated everything than in discovering where he fails, contradicts himself, becomes strange, becomes ordinary, or becomes impossible to classify.

items.fullDescription: REMINDER: SEPTEMBER 22 SUBMISSION DEADLINE American Comparative Literature Association 2027 Annual Meeting University of Houston May 20-23 The Poverty of Literature Organizer: Gabriel Quigley, University of Victoria (gabrielquigley@uvic.ca) How does literature represent poverty? Is poverty available for representation? The title of this seminar is taken from Marx's The Poverty of Philosophy, which, in turn, subverts Proudhon's The Philosophy of Poverty. In it, Marx critiques the approach taken by Proudhon and other anarchist, communist, or socialist "theoreticians" who assume that economic categories exist independently of history. According to Marx, "so long as they look for science and merely make systems, so long as they are at the beginning of the struggle, they see in poverty nothing but poverty, without seeing in it the revolutionary, subversive side, which will overthrow the old society." A similar critique might be leveled at today's writers and critics: when literature and literary criticism engage with poverty at all, do they merely reduce it to an ahistorical economic category? What forms of reification, alienation, and exploitation does the literary assumption that poverty is available for representation produce? This seminar asks what literature owes to people experiencing poverty. At a time when 847 million people live in extreme poverty-95% of whom are in the Global South-it seeks to bring together research on the representation, history, and ontological status of poverty. Unlike Marx's "theoreticians," who "see in poverty nothing but poverty," scholars analyzing poverty through other frameworks-such as ethical demand, affective complexity, geopolitical disparities, aesthetic fetishization, and state failure-are strongly encouraged to submit abstracts. Papers may respond to such questions as: how should poverty be represented, if at all? Beyond an economic category, can poverty be conceived as an aesthetic, metaphysical, or phenomenological category? How is the concept of poverty entangled with conceptions of lack, deprivation, or destitution? How does the global distribution of poverty reflect the ongoing injuries of imperialism, colonialism, neocolonialism, globalization, and ecological catastrophe? Possible topics: - Poverty and realism; poverty and genre - The ethics of speaking for the poor - Testimony, life writing, and first-person accounts of poverty - Poverty and racial capitalism - Postcolonial and decolonial frameworks for poverty - Poverty and ecological catastrophe; climate precarity - Poverty and intersectionality (race, gender, sexuality, disability) - "Poverty porn," sentimentality, and voyeurism - Working-class literature and labor - Poverty in the Global South; imperialism and uneven development - Urban and rural poverty as literary landscapes - Homelessness and houselessness - Poverty and the archive - Poverty and affect: shame, solidarity, rage - The literary canon and class; institutional gatekeeping - Austerity, welfare, and the state in literature - Migration, displacement, and border crossing - Literature and human rights - Poverty as aesthetic, metaphysical, or phenomenological category - Poverty and ontology; being, lack, and deprivation - Bare life and destitution ACLA Seminar Description can be accessed here: https://www.acla.org/seminar/63e1eb87-fe99-49c9-aac0-517ccf904102. items.fullDescription: 2027 National Advanced Writing Symposium "Evolving Possibilities: Futures of Advanced Writing" FREE & ONLINE, Hosted by the University of Southern California Event Date: Friday, January 29, 2027 Deadline to Submit a Proposal: Friday, September 25, 2026 Link to Submit a Proposal: https://docs.google.com/forms/d/e/1FAIpQLSd9dZiyi_mlo-G9bYPmj47EmQg07M_Xv83yap4bkd_q0i73EQ/viewform Context The USC Writing Program is delighted to host the fourth annual National Advanced Writing Symposium! The event is entirely ONLINE and FREE to both speakers and attendees, as we aim to bring together teachers of advanced and/or upper-division college composition courses to discuss innovative methods and effective practices. Our theme, "Evolving Possibilities: Futures of Advanced Writing," welcomes participants to contemplate how Advanced Writing will address emerging needs and conditions in our discipline and beyond. Please join us and share your work in the Advanced Writing space. We hope to include a wide variety of topics, from how you theorize modes of writing beyond first-year composition to how you build your students' confidence and skills as they prepare to write in a rapidly changing, professional world beyond college. Our theme invites analyses of the multifaceted information landscapes that advanced student writers face as they transition from school writers to life writers. If selected to present at the symposium, you will also be invited to submit your work to the NAWS Online Journal , which will publish its inaugural issue in Fall 2027. Topics & Issues We welcome proposals for panels, individual presentations, workshops, and roundtables related to any of the following: The Human: How can we prioritize the humanity of knowledge production in Advanced Writing contexts? Humanist futures; innovations that embrace analog or paper-based practices; reimagining low-tech approaches; the paradox of reclaiming techniques of the past to offset the uncertainties of emerging technologies. The Generative: How is the humanity of writing in conversation with digital generative tools? Human generation versus machine synthesis; generative AI and LLMs, including contrasting views on these technologies and debates over their uses; writing as generative (because certainly, writing was generative before Chat GPT!) The Political: How can Advanced Writing pedagogies resist oppression, increase inclusion, and support social justice? items.fullDescription: This call is for panelists to present on an approved in-person NeMLA 2027 panel on "The Gothic Servant." While the Gothic has long been associated with monsters, haunted houses, unstable hierarchies, and hidden knowledge, the servant's specific connections to the genre's core dynamics of space, affect, and plot have been critically undertheorized. Yet Gothic narratives fundamentally depend upon servant figures to produce narrative tension, mediate hidden knowledge, and expose the instability of domestic, social, and political order. This panel therefore positions the Gothic servant not as a supplementary character but as a central Gothic mechanism and epistemological problem worthy of scholarly attention and analysis. We invite panelists to consider the following types of questions: In what ways does the servant function as a Gothic mechanism, producing narrative tension, circulating forbidden knowledge, and exposing the instability of domestic and class order? How do the servant's social and/or affective roles (as caregiver, confidante, observer, jailer, etc.) shape Gothic plots and complicate power hierarchies within Gothic narratives? How does the servant's structural invisibility produce, rather than merely reflect, Gothic preoccupations with spectrality, repression, identity and/or power? Topics may include but are not limited to: servants as uncanny, spectral, or monstrous figures; servants as central to Gothic plot and narrative structure; servants, secrecy, and forbidden knowledge; race, coloniality, and servitude in imperial and postcolonial Gothic; invisibility and the Gothic politics of service; servant figures in contemporary Gothic; and the afterlives of Gothic servant characters in adaptation and other media. We welcome papers on servant characters in Gothic texts from the mid-nineteenth century to the present, from any geographical area. All abstract submissions must be submitted through the NeMLA portal. When doing so, please submit to panel 22348, "The Gothic Servant" (https://cfplist.com/nemla/Home/S/22348).

items.fullDescription: Dans un contexte marqué par l'expansion des environnements numériques, les processus d'autonomisation des communautés se redéfinissent en profondeur. La culture numérique ne se réduit plus à un ensemble d'outils techniques : elle constitue désormais un espace dynamique de production, de circulation et de légitimation des savoirs, notamment locaux. À travers ces mutations, les communautés accèdent à de nouvelles formes de visibilité et de reconnaissance, leur permettant de s'affirmer comme actrices de leur propre développement. En mobilisant leurs ressources culturelles, symboliques et sociales, elles investissent les espaces numériques pour produire du sens, partager leurs expériences et renforcer leur pouvoir d'agir. Cette session propose d'examiner les articulations entre culture numérique, pratiques participatives et autonomisation, en mettant l'accent sur les formes émergentes d'engagement collectif médiatisé. Elle s'intéresse en particulier aux dispositifs numériques qui privilégient la co-création, la collaboration et l'innovation sociale, tout en interrogeant les conditions de leur appropriation. Dans cette perspective, l'autonomisation ne relève pas uniquement d'une capacité individuelle, mais s'inscrit dans des collectifs dynamiques, où les communautés développent des stratégies d'usage et de réappropriation du numérique afin de répondre à leurs besoins, valoriser leur patrimoine et consolider leur résilience face aux transformations contemporaines.

items.fullDescription: The term "transgressive fiction" was coined in 1993 by LA Times columnist Michael Silverblatt to describe a loosely related coterie of authors in the '80s and '90s whose writing has "violation at its core: violation of norms, of humanistic enterprise, of the body." Silverblatt's preliminary "sketch" of the genre's leading voices was primarily American, almost entirely Anglophone, and exclusively white. Since its coinage both the term and the archive it describes have widened to include both a more diverse set of contemporary Anglo-American authors and a broader set of transnational and transtemporal texts. In both academic and popular contexts "transgressive fiction" has come to loosely describe Anglo-American authors from Samuel R. Delany to J.G. Ballard, non-Anglophone writers like Ry? Murakami and Virginie Despentes, and historical antecedents ranging from Petronius's Satyricon to the writings of the Marquis de Sade. The para-academic provenance of "transgressive fiction" as a term and its liberal application, especially by non-scholarly readers, to a wide range of culturally and historically distinct texts make it a problematic, yet perhaps fruitful, term for academic, historicist scholarship. This panel proposes both to interrogate the risks and benefits of "transgressive fiction" as a scholarly rubric, as well as a bid to further widen its archive by considering neglected texts from across space and time that might, however loosely, be identified as transgressive fictions. Proposals might ask: Why (not) use "transgressive fiction" over alternative terms like "blank fiction" (Annesley, Caveney, Young), "aggressive fiction" (Hume) or "queer experimental fiction" (Bradway)? What do we, as scholars or readers, wish to find transgressed by such fiction? Is the heterogeny of transgressive fiction's archive part of its transgressive appeal? What neglected texts ought to be considered in the lineage of transgressive fiction? What contemporary texts resonate with its organizing principles? Submissions accepted until September 20th, 2026. Despite recent efforts to decolonize institutions and collections, many archival practices were developed in ways that contribute to this tension while introducing ethical and epistemological questions that complicate our ability to read archives as authoritative collections. Decisions about selection, description, curation, organization, and exhibition have vital implications for access and the construction of narrative within the archive. By questioning these practices as a series of choices and attitudes, scholars can arrive at a more meaningful understanding of how they enable and frustrate different kinds of knowledge production. How are researchers and students interacting with these archival materials in ways that reinforce and challenge Western epistemologies? How do the ways that publics access and interact with archival collections and exhibits shape cultural knowledge and memory? How does a lack of access condition or obstruct agency in ways that constrain social change? Please submit a 250-300 word abstract through the NeMLA portal for consideration. items.fullDescription: Critical disability studies and the medical humanities have generated growing interest within cultural and literary studies in the past decade. Yet scholars in these fields tend to engage with disability and illness either thematically, examining their representations in literary and cultural productions, or rhetorically, tracing how they inflect the very form of these productions. Rarely do such approaches ask how disability and illness might transform criticism itself, that is, how neurodivergent or mad cognition might become a critical resource, transforming the ways we read, analyze, and inhabit literary and cultural studies. This panel invites papers that take up this question, exploring what new methodologies neurodivergence and mental illness-including, but not limited to, autism, ADHD, schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, OCD, PTSD, and depression-can generate. How might neurodivergent and mad ways of thinking and being-in-the-world produce innovative, crip approaches to literary and cultural analysis that refuse sane- and neuronormative standards? Such a project finds grounding in Arseli Dokumaci's concept of disability-as-method, "a creative approach through which research methods are informed by, modeled after, and tailored to the situated knowledges of disabled people" (Activist Affordances, 11). It also resonates with Robert McRuer's call to challenge "straight composition, with its demand for composed and docile texts, skills, and bodies" (Crip Theory, 171), as well as with Jack Halberstam's notion of low theory, a voluntarily undisciplined mode of knowledge that defies the linearity and restraint of established academic discourse (The Queer Art of Failure). We welcome papers that generate or point toward new critical approaches grounded in neurodivergent and mad cognition and cripped methodologies. We particularly encourage submissions in which such cognition is presented as an embodied epistemological standpoint where neurodivergent or mad experience shapes the work from within, rather than serving as a structuring metaphor.

items.fullDescription: The digital infrastructure in today's world mirrors the colonial administrative structure with its control over data, policing user's behavior, and pushing narratives for the majoritarian political power. The global tech giants have as much sway in geopolitics as the global leaders themselves. Previously the conditions of colonization created an unequal economic infrastructure that marginalizes the local communities, and even after independence from the colonial power, the trade relations remain that of a colonial appendage. Similarly, the upkeep of the digital sphere is not without its economic and environmental hazards. Anibal Quijano (1928-2018) a Peruvian sociologist, talks about the plight of this expansion for resources in his book, On the Coloniality of Power. He says: …the contemporary scientific community, insists on destroying the conditions for life on the planet. So, both the movement of the most subjugated people in this world, those who would not be able to exist if they sold their means of subsistence, and those who realize that if all this comes to an end no one will be able to survive, come together in a shared analysis. 359 He stresses on the role of the communities who've resisted the colonial and postcolonial measures to protect their land, water, and air over the years. It shows how the communities have more of a lateral structure which allows for debate and discussions as opposed to the hierarchy of the colonial administrative infrastructure. This panel seeks to garner discourse around the digital world's ambivalent nature of enhancing global communications and generating jobs at the cost of endangering local communities. items.fullDescription: Jordan Peele's Us is a critically acclaimed horror original about government-manufactured clones that are forced to mimic the lives of the people who live on the surface like stringless puppets. While Peele focuses more on a physical tethering, there is a psychological tethering that can be gleamed from this piece, specifically as it relates to the idea of double consciousness. In his work "The Striving of the Negro People," W.E.B. Du Bois describes this idea as "this sense of always looking at oneself through the eyes of others, of measuring one's soul by the tape of a world that looks on in amused contempt or pity. One ever feels his two-ness-an American, a Negro, two souls, two thoughts, two unreconciled strivings; two warring ideals in one dark body, whose dogged strength alone keeps it from being torn asunder." These "warring ideas" can exist in any group as the numerous stereotypes, prejudices, and misconceptions alive and well in the world has convinced many to fashion a Franksteined-version of themselves in the hopes of being accepted or safe. The jerky, uncoordinated movements of the tethered from the movie are the perfect metaphor for this forced reality. People attempting to push themselves to live in ways they were not meant to and should not have to. This panel is asking participants to provide submissions that explore the many ways this "tethering" has manifested in the world and explain the impact had on people's lives or how this knowledge can be used as a way to empower people and bring communities together. In other words, in what ways could we be tethered to unfair or unjust interpretations in the world and/or how could our lived experiences be used to untether us from opinions and views that do not empower us and help us build healthy communities? The chair welcomes essays, critical analysis, creative non-fiction, hybrid works, and excerpts of longer pieces.

items.excerpt: In the United States, our lives are marked by an abundance of convenience. items.fullDescription: In the United States, our lives are marked by an abundance of convenience. From fresh produce year-round to two-day shipping, convenient choices feel soft, easy, and frictionless, as they have specifically been engineered to feel. Until relatively recently, it has been possible to maintain a cultural and systemic sense of alienation that makes the cost of our convenience invisible to us-to localize all of the necessary precarity and exploitation for convenience "somewhere else," (often in the Global South) and then to ignore it. However, the veil is lifting, and "somewhere else" has reached us directly--worker and labor exploitation, droughts and systemic extermination of wild animals, widening class gaps, heat waves, short and snowless winters, floods, wildfires, unprecedented weather patterns, booming microbe populations that alter the very soil we stand on. A sustainable future must be an inconvenient one, and perhaps a precarious one, unless we can remake communities with a focus on outmoded forms of convenience: reciprocity, mutual aid, de-suburbanization, and anti-capitalism. In this panel, we hope to facilitate a conversation about art, in/convenience, precarity, and resistance in community. We also hope to consider alternate views of in/convenience: What can we do to create communities in which the inconvenience of slowness is celebrated rather than derided? How can we utilize writing to grieve futures that didn't materialize? How might we create work that celebrates the pleasure of systemic and interpersonal inconvenience? How can we build resilience to inconvenience and precarity at once, together? In the tradition of scholars and writers like Lauren Berlant, Hanif Abdurraqib, Anna Lowenhaupt Tsing, and Margaret Price, how can we embrace the inconvenient as a site of connection and resistance? We welcome writers of creative nonfiction, poetry, fiction, art pieces, and hybrid works who seek to consider community and in/convenience. We are looking for writing about all forms of convenience and inconvenience, from the granular to the esoteric. After panelists share their work, the chairs will facilitate a conversation between writers and audience members.

items.location: Salve Regina University. Newport, Rhode Island · NEMLA
items.excerpt: Education is an ideal means of empowerment, for it enables students to take ownership of the historical and personal archives that stand for their communities. items.fullDescription: Education is an ideal means of empowerment, for it enables students to take ownership of the historical and personal archives that stand for their communities. This panel regards the classroom as a privileged site of such empowerment-particularly for students from immigrant families-and seeks proposals on how to equip them to become active agents in producing their own interpretations of the cultural and spatial memory they share with their forebears. We draw inspiration from courses in which students articulate their personal, familial, and communal relationships with the tangible and intangible spaces of the city they inhabit: from their own homes to the streets they traverse daily, the buildings, neighborhoods, and monuments they encounter, and the individual and social practices that animate them. Setting their lived experience against the historical archives that purport to represent them, students produce analytical descriptions of urban space. Their work collectively assembles a shared repository of cultural memory - a "counter-archive" that weaves together place-based learning, immigration histories, and autobiographical narrative. In classrooms of diverse composition, this work empowers along more than one path. Immigrant students illuminate the place of their communities within the urban social fabric, while others discover-in their own projects and in those of their classmates-insights that transform how they perceive the city and their own identities in relation to it. We invite educators across languages, periods, and disciplines to share pedagogical projects and activities-assignments, archives, community-engaged work, digital repositories, creative and testimonial writing-that treat teaching as a practice of empowerment. We especially welcome contributions that reflect on the theory of change behind their work: when does a classroom project produce agency, and how do we know?

items.fullDescription: Call for Papers NeMLA's 58th Annual Convention - "Empowering Communities" March 6-9, 2027 | Salve Regina University, Newport, Rhode Island (Hybrid Conference) Panel Title: Tracing Female Body, Art & Economy in the Global South Primary Area / Secondary Area: Women's and Gender Studies / Interdisciplinary Humanities Modality: Hybrid Chair: Maryam Raza (University of Auckland, New Zealand) This panel explores how the historical treatment of female bodies in the Global South through the patriarchal structures of subjectification, commodification, sexualization and objectification has been reversed by contemporary strategies of resistance and reclamation. Women increasingly reconfigure the female body through carnivalesque, alternative spaces of identity, creativity and skill through embodied forms. The female body evolves from a passive object of desire into an active, expressive, and economically productive site. Thus, women transform spaces of suppression to places of resistance and empowerment. Hussain et al. (2025) note that emancipation precedes autonomy and decision-making in socio-economic spheres. The panel further examines the intersection of bodily narratives with performative femininity, wellness cultures, fitness regimes, and beauty and anti-aging industries. It also restructures the domestic space as a site of culinary entrepreneurship, aided by digital platforms. Consequently, the Global South woman utilizes such arenas to enhance visibility, economic upward mobility, and global networks beyond what Fahmida Riaz termed the "Four Walled Homestead." items.fullDescription: This panel invites papers that examine the agency of marginalized characters in literary, visual, audiovisual, and artistic productions from the French?speaking world across any historical period. Artistic works offer numerous examples of figures who maintain an ambivalent relationship to their communities. Because of their social or ethnic origins, their divergent perspectives, or their transgression of established norms, certain characters find themselves pushed to the margins of social, familial, or professional groups. While such exclusion may appear to weaken those who experience it, this panel asks whether marginalization might also function as a source of strength. Can marginality become a generative position? Do marginalized individuals succeed in forming new communities that enable them to confront stigma and ultimately overcome it? This discussion seeks to shift our understanding of the place occupied by marginalized individuals and groups in fictional narratives. By considering the networks of solidarity that emerge among marginalized subjects, the panel explores what lies beneath their presumed inferiority, inviting critical attention to what is hidden, erased, or rendered invisible within dominant narratives. More importantly, we will examine how marginalized communities may become empowering spaces of resistance, mutual support, and hope. Drawing on approaches from cultural studies, postcolonial theory, sociolinguistics, and intersectionality, this session seeks to understand how literary, visual, audiovisual, and artistic narratives stage the tensions between marginality and belonging, strength and vulnerability. Proposals engaging with environmental humanities, posthumanism, Indigenous studies, as well as diaspora and migration studies are strongly encouraged. We also welcome submissions drawing on gender and queer studies, memory and trauma studies, digital humanities, or other interdisciplinary frameworks within the humanities. We welcome proposals of 250-300 words, in French or English, submitted by September 30.

In an era marked by migration, political polarization, social fragmentation, environmental crisis, and renewed struggles for collective empowerment, narratives of masculinity have become central sites through which communities negotiate belonging, responsibility, vulnerability, and resistance. While dominant models of masculinity have often been associated with hierarchy, authority, nationalism, and exclusion, contemporary world literatures increasingly depict alternative masculinities grounded in care, ethical responsibility, emotional openness, solidarity, and collective survival. Such representations challenge inherited structures of power while opening new possibilities for community formation and social transformation. This panel invites comparative and transnational approaches that explore how literary texts, films, cultural narratives, and other expressive forms construct, critique, or reimagine masculinities within local and global communities. Particular attention may be given to how gender intersects with race, class, migration, coloniality, religion, ecology, technology, and cultural memory in shaping collective identities and practices of empowerment. Situated within the broader concerns of World Literature and Comparative Literature, this session seeks to foster dialogue across regions, languages, and traditions while investigating how masculinities participate in the creation-or disruption-of empowered communities. items.fullDescription: Call for Papers: Geographies of Horror Department of English Studies (University of Zadar) in collaboration with The Society for the Study of the American Gothic (SSAG) Keynote speaker: Jeffrey Andrew Weinstock (Central Michigan University) May 20-21st 2027, University of Zadar (Zadar, Croatia) The study of horror has always been inseparable from the question of space. From the shadowed corridors of Gothic castles to contemporary digital voids, spaces in horror are never just passive backdrops. They function as active agents that shape perception, destabilize subjectivity, and collapse the distinction between interior and exterior, revealing how fragile our sense of spatial coherence can be. This conference seeks to understand how spaces become haunted - materially, symbolically, psychologically, and technologically, and how these hauntings articulate broader cultural anxieties, historical traumas, and epistemological uncertainties. In Gothic and horror traditions, fear unfolds through space, guiding perception, and encounters with the unknown. Early Gothic forms, such as castles and monasteries, establish models of spatial excess, enclosure, and architectural anxiety, while the haunted house transforms domestic familiarity into something uncanny. In modern and contemporary horror, this logic extends to urban environments, where entire cities and infrastructures become haunted. While urban legends and other unsettling narratives embed fear in everyday life, abandoned malls, transit systems, and brutalist structures evoke concepts such as "non-places," characterized by transience and anonymity. At the same time, horror increasingly stages the breakdown of spatial logic itself. Non-Euclidean geometries, infinite corridors, and paradoxical environments destabilize perception and challenge epistemological certainty. In these instances, space becomes fundamentally unknowable, aligning with cosmic horror and philosophical pessimism. These concerns extend into digital and virtual environments, where video games, online narratives, and immersive technologies generate new forms of spatial horror. Phenomena such as The Backrooms exemplify liminal, endlessly reproducible environments that evoke both familiarity and existential dread. Simultaneously, haunted space becomes internalized within the body and mind, as psychological and body horror depict interiority as fragmented and invasive. With all this in mind, we welcome papers from across disciplines and media that examine the spatial dimensions of horror, including but not limited to: Gothic and classical haunted spaces Urban and infrastructural hauntings, including "non-places" Non-Euclidean, paradoxical, and incoherent spatialities Digital and virtual environments (games, online narratives, immersive media) The body and subjectivity as haunted spaces Ecological and environmental horror Spatial storytelling across literature, film, television, comics, and interactive media The keynote speaker for the event will be Professor Jeffrey Andrew Weinstock (Central Michigan University). He is a Professor of English at Central Michigan University, where he teaches a range of courses on American literature and popular culture. He is the founder and president of The Society for the Study of the American Gothic, the founder and general editor of the peer-reviewed journal American Gothic Studies, and the co-founder and past chair of the Modern Language Association Gothic Studies Forum. He also serves as the associate editor in charge of horror for the Los Angeles Review of Books and is currently the general editor for Bloomsbury Publishing's six-volume Cultural History of Monsters series. His research focuses on the "cultural work" performed by the Gothic in its various manifestations - the ways in which Gothic texts and practices give shape to culturally specific anxieties and desires. This interest has led him from considering, for example, how nineteenth-and early twentieth-century American women made use of Gothic conventions as a strategy to express discontentment with their circumscribed roles to thinking about the ways contemporary monsters reflect shifting American fears and aspirations. To date, he is the author or editor of 34 books and more than 100 essays and book chapters on the Gothic, American literature, cult film, and popular culture. Abstracts of 250-300 words, accompanied by a short bio (approximately 100 words) and 3-5 keywords, should be submitted to geographyhorror@gmail.com . The deadline for the abstract submission is October 1st 2026. Selected papers focused on American Gothic and horror themes will also be considered for publication in the American Gothic Studies Journal.

items.fullDescription: CALL FOR PRESENTATION PAPER ABSTRACTS "Are Karl Marx's 'Perpetuum Mobile' and/or Max Weber's 'Machine State' Dominating Labor Today? Why or Why Not?" Students, researchers, faculty members, and scholars working in sociology and related social sciences are invited to submit conference presentation paper abstracts for an open conference session entitled "Are Karl Marx's 'Perpetuum Mobile' and/or Max Weber's 'Machine State' Dominating Labor Today? Why or Why Not?" The session will be part of the XXI International Sociological Association (ISA) World Congress of Sociology, from July 4-10, 2027, at Chonnam National University in Jeonnam-Gwangju Special Metropolitan City, Korea. Karl Marx and Max Weber both thought about a time when machines would dominate labor. Marx wrote of a "perpetuum mobile" to describe the unceasing turnover of money by a machine of indestructible materiality, circulating a repeating and alternating flow of sale and purchase. Max Weber's "Sociology of Domination" theory warned that the power to coerce markets endlessly would cause endless conflicts. For Marx social change entailed communist revolution, while Weber, who was not a Marxist, worried that social change would be constricted to political coups to control the government's informational infrastructure. Social problems of alienation and rationalization, capitalist wealth and inequality, abuse of power and authority, coerced markets, money hording and social stratification are as alive today as when Marx and Weber set down theories about these social problems over a hundred years ago. What can we say about our AI dominated world using the concepts and writings of Marx and Weber today? Do their economic and historical comparative concepts help us understand our digital world? Why or why not? Submit presentation abstracts by October 14, 2026, through the ISA Congress Submission System link below. items.fullDescription: Since the widespread emergence of Generative AI a few years ago, educators across disciplines have been reconsidering how technology shapes teaching, learning, writing, and assessment. While some departments and faculty have leaned into these new Large Language Models and the technological "advances" they offer, others have worked just as diligently to keep AI out of their classrooms. In light of the recent ban on GenAI in K-8 classrooms by New York City Public Schools, it is possible that the tides in education are going to shift away from AI and back to the uniquely human approach to education. As institutions and educators continue to debate the role of GenAI in education, questions about how to teach effectively without these technologies have become increasingly important. I am currently seeking contributions from interdisciplinary teachers and scholars for a proposed collection on "Teaching without GenAI in the Age of AI." This volume aims to explore pedagogical strategies for instructing without AI. While recent publications look at how to incorporate AI into writing instruction or discuss the complicated nuances of AI in writing classrooms, there is a gap in the field regarding practical approaches on how to instruct without AI in the classroom. Questions to consider include: - How have you structured assignments to prevent AI from being used? - How has your discipline been affected by AI, and how have you worked to keep it out of your classroom? - What pedagogical, disciplinary, ethical, or learning goals motivate your decision to teach without generative AI? - What are your success stories, or failures, of teaching without AI? - How are your students responding to work without AI? - What policies, structures, or pedagogical practices have you used to discourage or prohibit unauthorized AI use? - Have you faced disciplinary contexts that make AI counterproductive? - What role does technology now play in your classroom? - Have you designed any pedagogical experiments or studies to assess your students' learning within a no-AI context? I invite contributions from teachers and scholars across disciplines and educational contexts, including K-12, higher education, and professional education. I am particularly interested in contributions that offer concrete strategies and resources for other educators to implement in their classrooms. Because this volume is intended to be a practical resource as well as a scholarly contribution, submissions that provide example assignments, lesson plans, classroom policies, assessment strategies, or other teaching materials are especially welcome. In order to make this resource available in a timely fashion and respond to existing publisher interest, please send an abstract of no more than 500 words and a brief biographical statement by October 15, 2026 to teachingwithoutgenai@gmail.com. Completed essays will be approximately 4,000 - 5,000 words and will be due by January 31, 2027.

items.fullDescription: European Comic Art Special Issue 'Francophone Graphic Narratives / Bande dessinée: Authority and Resistance' European Comic Art invites proposals for a special issue on 'Francophone Graphic Narratives/Bande dessinée: Authority and Resistance'. This issue will examine how francophone graphic narratives engage with, challenge, and reimagine authority in its many forms - political, cultural, institutional, and aesthetic - and how they forge practices of resistance and dissent. The bande dessinée is a medium that subverts hierarchies and blurs boundaries. Long regarded as the lowly offspring of literature and the visual arts, comics have since been legitimised by scholars and artists demonstrating their capacity to engage with complex sociohistorical, political, and cultural topics. This 'Ninth Art' now occupies an increasingly important place in university classrooms, academic publications, and public discourse alike. Its multimodal features - panel layout, gutters, framing, braiding, and complex interplay between text and image - allow comics to stage and challenge authority in formally distinctive ways. This aesthetic vantage point makes comics a powerful medium through which to bring displaced, excluded, and silenced narratives into view. From Chantal Montellier's impressive four-decade oeuvre of political cartoons and graphic novels contesting racism, misogyny and totalitarianism to Jessica Oublié's Peyi an nou , which provides a counternarrative to state discourse on the BUMIDOM, the bande dessinée has often served to undercut official rhetoric. This special issue of European Comic Art seeks articles that examine how Francophone bandes dessinées engage with dominant institutions and discourses from theoretical and pedagogical perspectives. How do comics represent power and powerlessness? How do they respond to hierarchies that exist in various settings and communities? How do they decentre and challenge 'standard' language practices? Finally, how might comics be used pedagogically to help foster students' critical thinking skills and question institutional, political, and social discourses? Possible topics include, but are not limited to: Migration Ecocriticism Social justice and political activism Gender and sexuality Comics and memory studies Class, labour, and economic inequality Pedagogy and second language acquisition Nationalism, cosmopolitanism, and globalization Colonial legacies, decolonial resistance/critique Monolingualism, multilingualism, and language politics Official histories, counter archives, and silenced narratives Humour, parody, satire, and subversion Submission Guidelines Please submit a 500-word abstract with a short biographical note to Liana Pshevorska at lpshevorska@wesleyan.edu and Valentina Denzel at vdenzel@msu.edu by October 15, 2026. Contributors may include up to four images, which will be factored into the overall length of the article. items.fullDescription: Digital Dirges: Video Games, Elegy, and the Rhetoric of Loss (McFarland, Studies in Gaming series) Editors: Marc A. Ouellette, Old Dominion University (mouellet@odu.edu) David Metzger, Old Dominion University (dmetzger@odu.edu) Project Overview: Video games are more likely to have a loss than a win condition. This means that players frequently confront a form that includes recursion, redemption, and repetition through a mode of elegiac literature. Thus, my panel will explore the interactive elegy offered by video games, both as a hermeneutic and a heuristic, which will be of use to literature scholars, creative writing instructors, and game designers alike. The current collection, then, explores the formal and thematic connections between the classical tradition of elegy-the discourse of mourning, loss, and remembrance-and the interactive medium of video games. Moving beyond traditional literary contexts, this volume argues that digital play actively constructs, mediates, and performs acts of mourning, remembrance (anamnesis), and fateful discovery (anagnorisis) essential to the elegy. Indeed, the classic arcade game, Missile Command, makes the player choose between protecting cities and defending missile bases. Its apocalyptic theme remains a common one as games have developed in terms of technologies and telling tales. Video games are, in fact, more likely to feature a loss than a win condition, meaning players frequently confront a form that includes recursion, redemption, and repetition through a distinctive mode of elegiac literature. As Classics scholar Michael Zimm (2019) argues, video games are now worthy of study based on their ability to produce compelling analogues of Greek literary forms. Indeed, in producing a literary narrative based on the reconciliation of mourning, masochism, and melancholia, video games comprise a previously unexplored area of elegiac literature. Beyond writing the lyrics of lament and loss, the player simultaneously interacts with and witnesses the dual literary processes of apotheosis (the attribution of divine or Christlike attributes, including releasing the divine through sacrifice) and anagnorisis (the literal "unignorancing" or moment of revelation of the means of dealing with the loss). Tellingly, video games, from Bioshock Infinite to Elder Scrolls to Red Dead Redemption, Gears of War, and Spec Ops games, to name just a few influential series, have taken up the traditional form of ritualized sacrifice and mourning. The act of losing, which is central to game design, is also a hallmark of elegiac prose (Regan 2017; Vickery 2009). The American elegy is a distinctive variant because of its emphasis on the one(s) left behind (Cavitch 2007), a precise entry point for games like The Last of Us, Dear Esther, and The Binding of Isaac. In games with strong allegories, like Dark Souls and Assassin's Creed, literal and figurative resurrection allows the game to combine quick apotheosis with the extended rhetorical work of anagnorisis, yielding a hybrid literary form. Thus, it remains to map and to theorize this emerging literary form. The peer-reviewed collection, Digital Dirges will explore the creation of the interactive elegy, both as hermeneutic and heuristic, since the player also participates in the literary process through an on-screen surrogate, adding yet another, unexplored, layer to the theorizing of an important literary form and its distinctive American literary variant. While the volume will contribute to Game Studies, it also offers a moment for the study of games to contribute to the understanding of established modes and forms. This exploration of the interactive elegy will be of use to literature scholars, creative writing instructors, and game designers alike. Topics may include but are not limited to discourses of gender in contexts of loss and the performance of mourning what games can teach us about narratives of mourning, and loss games, grief, melancholia, masochism and mourning the contradictory pleasures of losing individual, communal and national loss games as prose, poetic or hybrid elegy games, loss and apotheosis the loss of childhood and/or innocence in games being the one left behind and the "redemption arc" resurrection and recursion games and the American elegy the elegiac mode in specific games and series digital writing and/or rhetoric and elegy psychoanalysis and elegy environmental design as a tombstone, how non-player characters (NPCs) function as mourners the effects of proximity to or complicity in acts of loss. teaching the elegy with games We invite scholars from multiple disciplines to submit abstracts (300-500 words by 16 Oct. 2026 with completed papers due 15 March 2027. Please send abstracts and inquiries to the editors.

items.fullDescription: Call for Papers: NANO: New American Notes Online (ISSN: 2160-0104) Special Issue 18: Exploring the Boundary Waters of the Blue Humanities Special Issue Guest Editors: Eric Denbang Kunkuri and Dana Van Kooy Deadline: 16 October 2026 Publication: spring/summer 2027 Full CFP Details: https://nanocrit.com/index.php/home/cfp-plus-submissions-new The creative and scholarly work being done in the blue humanities has deepened our turn towards exploring waterways and boundary waters. The currents circulating through the blue humanities flow into and from myriad disciplines, including anthropology, biology, decolonial studies, feminist/queer studies, geography, history, indigenous studies, literature, music, performance studies, philosophy, and the visual arts. The cultural and theoretical inlets being carved out by work in the blue humanities have proven generative in terms of developing a distinctive metaphor-laden language, analytic methods like Kamau Brathwaite's theory of "tidalectics," and new ways of submerging ourselves in both historical and unprecedented questions about the water that is in and, as Rachel Carson notes in her famous title, "around us." For this special issue, we invite submissions of traditional and multimodal essays of up to 5,000 words (excluding works cited) that explore the boundary waters of the blue humanities. We encourage essays focused on narratives as well as submissions that explore art installations and other medial forms that address the boundary waters circulating around and through the blue humanities. Topics may include but are not limited to the following: Boundary waters that divide and connect nations, classes, and/or ecological zones Mythic, cinematic, and visual narratives of how humans and/or nonhumans are "held," migrate, or are moved through watery littorals Critical explorations like those associated with "tidalectics," a term that comes from Kamau Brathwaite, who proposed an alternative framework for literary and political engagement that is grounded in the rhythm of waves and the cyclic ebb and flow of tides "Portraits" of littoral space(s) in literature, history, myth, the visual arts, and theatrical and musical performances Exploring the significance of physical, structural, and emotional vulnerabilities and instabilities within littorals, shoals, or port cities Hydrological infrastructure (colonial, postcolonial, urban, rural) associated with port cities, canal locks, and dams Relational undercurrents that speak to our ways of submerging ourselves into the watery worlds that surround us Traditional water ways: ways of being with or "holding" water The role of inland waterways in routing stories and/or facilitating/impeding human and nonhuman migrations Exploring the agency of oceans and rivers in sustaining capitalist and imperial economies and their alternatives Water's many forms (snow, ice, fog, rivers, oceans) and ways "water" facilitates connection and/or imposes isolation How waterways-"paths" of water and ways of being with water-lead us to new or alternative futures Scenes of erosion that expose lost or forgotten histories Please items.fullDescription: Call for Chapters Proposals Submission Deadline: July 17, 2026 Full Chapters Due: October 30, 2026 Submission Date: October 30, 2026 Introduction This edited collection features scholarly voices with attention to horror in its transmedia representations, including film, literature, comics, art, branding, and more. Chapters give attention to the ways that fans take up the realities and ideas presented in horror, the affordances of the genre, and participation in this network of storytelling. The reactions of readers/viewers/fans, the decisions of creatives, the presentation of ideas within particular forms of media, and more form elements of the researched conversation in this volume. Objective This collection seeks to advance conversation about the theoretical functions of horror across media including notions of adaptation and literary/literacy-based choices in the work. This includes, but is not limited to, design structures, cultural influences, the role of lore, (re)considerations of the monstrous, embodiment in the genre, sub-genre considerations, and more. Students enrolled in courses in these fields can benefit from this knowledge as they pursue courses of study and further academic work in these disciplines. items.fullDescription: CALL FOR CHAPTERS The Handbook of Boredom in Modern Literature Editors: Mariusz Finkielsztein (University of Gdan?sk) mariusz.finkielsztein@gmail.com Josefa Ros Velasco (Complutense University of Madrid) josros@ucm.es The Handbook of Boredom in Modern Literature is to be a comprehensive monographic study examining boredom as a central aesthetic, philosophical, psychological, and socio-cultural category in the history of modern literature. Rather than relying purely on abstract theory, this volume approaches boredom through focused case studies devoted to individual authors and their works. Across these chapters, boredom-alongside adjacent states such as ennui, tedium, spleen, acedia, melancholy, existential malaise, and affective exhaustion-emerges variously as paralysis, protest, privilege, illness, and spiritual crisis. By situating close textual readings within the broader intellectual history of modernity, the volume, written by a multidisciplinary group of authors, is to demonstrate that literary boredom is a powerful diagnostic lens on social order, temporality, and the modern subject's experience of meaninglessness. Volume Structure & Epochal Scope The volume is planned as a Handbook or Companion and covers not only the most vital writers addressing the theme of boredom but also a broad selection of modern authors (around 60 chapters). The book is to trace the evolution of literary boredom across (tentatively) seven historical and thematic phases: Early Modernity & Enlightenment Foundations: Early reflections on existential void and social routine (e.g. Diderot, Laclos, Austen). Romantic Ennui (1770s-1840s): Melancholy, idealist frustration, and the world-weary anti-hero (e.g., Goethe, de Stae?l, Senancour, Byron, Chateaubriand, Constant, Stendhal, Sand, Balzac, Musset). The Superfluous Man: The Russian literary archetype of social paralysis, alienation, and unfulfilled potential (e.g. Pushkin, Lermontov, Goncharov, Turgenev). Bourgeois Boredom, Realism, & Decadent Spleen: Domestic stagnation, industrial monotony, social entrapment, and aesthetic decay (e.g., Dickens, Flaubert, Tolstoy, Fontane, Chopin, Ibsen, Gilman, Conrad, Chekhov, Baudelaire, Huysmans, Wilde). Modernist Stagnation (Early 20th C.): Temporal distortion, consciousness, alienation, and metaphysical paralysis (e.g., Proust, Joyce, Pessoa, Mann, Kafka, Woolf). Catastrophism & Existential Absurdity (Mid-20th C.): Totalitarian dread, the absurdity of existence, and postwar existential malaise (e.g., Broch, Platonov, Orwell, H. Miller, Gombrowicz, Sartre, Camus, Beckett, Buzzati, Gracq). Postwar Emptiness, Consumerism, & Digital Fatigue: Mass society, late-capitalist hyper-consumption, information overload, and contemporary affective exhaustion (e.g., Moravia, Perec, de Beauvoir, Ernaux, Bellow, Bernhard, Duras, DeLillo, Houellebecq, Ferrante, Rourke, Moshfegh). Chapter Guidelines & Scope Each chapter must offer an in-depth analysis of the theme of broadly understood boredom in the work of a single author (according to a formula: Boredom in...). The title should include the name and surname of a writer as a main part, and a freely formulated subtitle. Analytical Approach: Authors may focus on a single representative work but should analyse boredom across multiple texts of an author to demonstrate how boredom functions as a recurring motif in the author's oeuvre. Target Audience: Written primarily for readers seeking to deepen their understanding of boredom in a specific author's work (spoilers are permitted), while remaining accessible to a general literary audience. Comparative analysis with other writers should be kept to a minimum. Required Contextual Elements: o Biographical Context: Key details situating the writer within their epoch. items.fullDescription: John Steinbeck once remarked that fellow-Californian Robinson Jeffers wrote some the "greatest poetry since Whitman." Steinbeck kept a significant collection of Jeffers work both in his personal library and Ed Ricketts' Lab, where Jeffers was an influential topic in their endlessly varied conversations. When asked about possibility of meeting the poet, Steinbeck declined with a telling degree of reverence: "His poetry is perfect to me, and I don't think one should get the man mixed up with his work." Although they did eventually meet-notably when Steinbeck lived in Monterey in 1944-their relationship was one of distant, though friendly, mutual respect. Although these two writers rarely crossed physical paths, their work maintains a wide concurrence of concern. They both deeply engaged with Californian geography and history; they both emphasized the influence of the natural world upon the individual and society; they both had social circles that revolved around the Monterey Peninsula; they both were interested in psychoanalytical theory; they both were students of classical literature and philosophy; they both experienced extraordinary recognition at the peak of their literary fame (at one point, Jeffers was on the cover of Time magazine); they both were deeply uncomfortable with such a cultural spotlight; they both admonished personal humility in the face of environmental forces. Intersections such as these (and many more) deserve to be explored with more depth and significance. The editorial staff at the Steinbeck Review invites submissions for a special edition, "John Steinbeck and Robinson Jeffers." We are particularly interested in perspectives which put these authors into conversation in productive and even unexpected ways. Although submissions are not required to examine both authors, we strongly suggest that they engage (even if briefly) both Steinbeck and Jeffers. We welcome all critical and theoretical perspectives. Please see the full guide for submissions here and submit your paper to the Steinbeck Review's online submission system, found at www.editorialmanager.com/Steinbeck, no later than October 31, 2026. Decisions will be made by December 1, 2026. Submissions should be accompanied by an abstract and key words.

items.fullDescription: Literary irony is a phenomenon that seems expressly invented for the approach Connotations: A Journal for Critical Debate (www.connotations.de) wishes to promote, namely combining the close reading of literary texts with wider theoretical perspectives. Clearly, irony is a textual feature, and it equally clearly reaches beyond individual texts in that it evokes and reflects basic constituents of human communication: in particular, the relationship between what is said and what is meant and the relationship between what is said and what is known. Irony comes into play when these relationships are marked by significant discrepancies. The discrepancy between what is said and what is meant is essential for verbal irony and the discrepancy between what is said and what is known is fundamental to dramatic (or narrative) irony. If and how these two kinds of irony belong together, however, is a moot point and one of the questions to be addressed by our symposium. Thus the unequal distribution of knowledge (between characters and/or between characters and the reader) which marks narrative and dramatic irony may be related to the divergence which characterizes verbal irony. When Viola in Shakespeare's Twelfth Night, disguised as a boy, says to Orsino: "I am all the daughters of my father's house," Orsino, who believes Viola to be a young man, must regard this statement as verbal irony on Viola's part. What is said ("daughters") is very different from what appears to be meant ("sons"). To us, the audience, however, this is a case of dramatic irony since we know that Viola is a woman and we observe Orsino's ignorance. What makes this case particularly intriguing is that here dramatic irony is not based on a discrepancy between what is said and what we know since Viola literally speaks the truth. The discrepancy arises between what we know and what is supposed to be spoken ironically. The example shows that asking about the relationship between verbal and dramatic/narrative irony entails numerous other questions that the Connotations symposium is going to address. In particular, we will ask about effects of irony, both with regard to characters and the audience. What is the added value of an ironic remark? What does it tell us about the speaker? In what way does an ironic utterance signal that there is a common ground between the communication partners? Are the inclusion and exclusion of others, i.e. those who get the ironical meaning and those who don't, similar to cases of discrepant awareness? How do we know that an utterance is meant ironically and how are we to deal with ambiguity in this respect? Can non-verbal irony markers be encoded in literary texts? Are theories of verbal irony based on notions of echo and pretence relatable to drama and fiction? We invite papers focussing on these and related questions, based on literature in English from the Middle Ages to the present. Please send an abstract (300 words max.) to the editors of Connotations at symposium2027@connotations.de by 31 October 2026

items.fullDescription: The Routledge Handbook of Hip Hop and Sport, Culture, and Activism Call for Chapters Description: The Routledge Handbook of Hip Hop and Sport, Culture and Activism addresses the critical need for a comprehensive academic survey of Hip Hop's connection to sport as a preeminent sociological and political force among Millennials and Generation Z. This handbook maps the emerging critical terrain where Hip Hop intersects with the sports-industrial complex, digital activism, and the persistent structures of racial capitalism and white supremacy. As the culture enters its second half-century, it serves as an emergent space for self-expression and identity formation, both to hegemonic and counter-hegemonic ends. The leading objectives of this volume are to delineate how Hip Hop's relationship with sport provides narrative resources for youth to explore their social realities in the context of late-stage capitalism and its bedfellows: white supremacy and patriarchy. This handbook explores both the route and roots of Hip Hop expression through the lens of the African diaspora and the historical relationship between Black expressive history and social movements. This handbook is also interested in the ways in which Hip Hop's relationship with sport can be oriented both towards liberation and political conservatism, particularly in the context of Hip Hop's historical and presentist embrace of Donald Trump and his representative movements. This project aims to both engage Hip Hop's historical relationship with sports (professional and amateur) as well as its contemporary shifts,such as the institutionalization of breaking in the 2024 Olympics and the rise of representation activism in major sports leagues (NBA, NFL) that create new tensions between cultural authenticity and corporate appropriation. It is intended to define the current state of theory and establish a foundation for future scholarship across the interdisciplinary fields of hip-hop studies, sport management, and Africana studies. Since this project is a handbook and not an anthology, the chapter topics have already been pre-selected by the editors. However, we encourage submissions that engage the specific areas of expertise of each contributor, and the contributor is welcome to interpret the proposed topics according to their own research and experience. The targeted audience for this handbook are advanced high school students and undergraduates, so chapters should be written with this audience in mind. We invite abstract submissions from Hip Hop practitioners, sport sociologists, scholars, graduate students, postgraduate researchers, and early career researchers. Authors will be notified of their acceptance by November 30th, 2026. Full chapters of 4,000-6,000 words (including references) are due by April 30th, 2027. For further questions, contact Dr. Micah J. Email the conference organizers at ncsa2027conference@gmail.com The Nineteenth-Century Studies Association (NCSA) invites proposals for 15-minute papers (300-word proposal) or complete panels of 3-4 papers (600-word proposal) that examine the shifting meanings and status of "the human" in the long nineteenth century-a period shaped by transformative scientific, social, and philosophical developments that continue to inform present-day thought. During this time, evolutionary theory and social Darwinism challenged the boundaries between humans and animals and raised new questions about human difference across race, class, and ethnicity. Theological and philosophical discourses reevaluated humanity's relationship to the divine, while pseudosciences such as phrenology, physiognomy, and anthropometry sought to codify human variation through tools of measurement often aligned with colonial and racial hierarchies. Advances in the natural sciences speculated on human origins and extraterrestrial life, situating "the human" within a larger cosmic framework. Industrialization redefined labor and bodily limits, generating anxieties about overpopulation, and paradoxically, race suicide and population extinction. Amid these pressures, labor and voting rights movements gained momentum, as marginalized groups fought for full inclusion. We welcome proposals from a variety of disciplines that engage with these and other transformations that redefined what it meant to be human-and to belong to humanity-across the long nineteenth century. Topics may include, but are not limited to: The influence of evolutionary theory on concepts of the human and the human/animal divide, including artistic and literary responses Scientific efforts to define human origins and difference through anthropology, racial theory, and other emerging disciplines Population anxieties related to degeneration, overpopulation, and demographic change Emancipated and enslaved bodies The effects of industrialization and technological advancement on understandings of the human body, labor, and automation The rise of the human sciences-psychology, physiology, and medicine-and new approaches to the mind and self Migration and the movement of people, and their impact on ideas of race, nation, and identity Secularization and shifting relationships between the human and the divine Changing human relationships to the environment and the nonhuman world Human rights, labor, and suffrage movements and the redefinition of personhood Transformations in education and access to knowledge The role of cultural institutions (museums, libraries, exhibitions) in shaping public and humanist discourse
