items.fullDescription: Call for Papers: [Children's and Young Adult Literature] at CEA 2027 Apr. 1-3, 2027 | St. Louis, Missouri The Westin St. Louis Hotel https://cea-web.org/the-conference-hotel The College English Association, a gathering of scholar-teachers in English studies, welcomes proposals for presentations on Children's and Young Adult Literature for our 57th annual conference. Submit your proposal at www.cea-web.org Scholars and teachers of children's and YA lit intimately know the transformative power the right story at the right time can have on an elementary, middle, or high school student. We do not need reminding of how words, and how they are communicated, to young learners have the ability to grow cognitive processes and lead to future generations of lovers of the written word and future torchbearers of the significance of those words coming from the minds of human beings. Coalescing around the conference theme, we consider how the influence of diverse sculpted stories opens the door to deeper discernment across the curriculum. Conference Theme: Gateways For its 2027 annual conference, the College English Association (CEA) invites proposals for papers and panels that explore the theme of "Gateways" and their significance in literature, criticism, and pedagogy. Tracing its history back to French explorers in the second half of the 18th century, the great city of St. Louis began as a fur trading post named after King Louis IX of France and was established on the ancestral lands of the Osage Nation, Missouria, and Illini Confederacy. Becoming part of the United States through the Louisiana Purchase of 1803, the city famously came to be known as the "Gateway to the West," serving as a launching point for generations of explorers and settlers expanding the frontier. Yet, we must remember that the city also serves as a gateway to its past as part of indigenous lands transformed through its colonial history into a major river port and trading center that fostered migration both outwards and inwards for centuries. Today, St. Louis invites us to reflect on the continued significance of gateways in our 21st-century lives. GENERAL CALL FOR PAPERS GATEWAYS: For its 2027 annual conference, the College English Association (CEA) invites proposals for papers and panels that explore the theme of "Gateways" and their significance in literature, criticism, and pedagogy. Potential areas of interest: How do gateways expand literary and cultural spaces but also, as access points, mark out boundaries and limits? Do gateways invite gatekeepers to enable and limit access? Is it possible to imagine gateways without gatekeepers? How can we imagine literary and cultural gateways to foster inter-cultural, cross-cultural, and trans-cultural interactions? How do we envision pedagogical approaches to create gateways for our students to new literary vistas, critical thought, and professional opportunities? How can gateways in both their physical and symbolic significances (like the city of St. Louis and the Gateway Arch) connect the territorial to the cultural, imaginative, and spiritual in literary-critical studies? In what ways can we re-imagine our scholarly and pedagogical work to open up interdisciplinary and multidisciplinary gateways? For CEA 2027, we are especially interested topics related to GATEWAYS in texts, disciplines, people, cultural studies, media, and pedagogy. Consider such topics as the implications of political gateways across time and place, cultural gateways of identity, gateways in the media (including social media) and how they impact society, pedagogical gateways of teaching philosophy and their implementation, or personal gateways through autobiography and memoir. GENERAL TOPICS: The CEA Conference encompasses a wide range of areas, including literary studies, creative writing, rhetoric and composition, technical communication, linguistics, and film. We further encourage proposals in areas about our wider role as academics, including student/instructor accountability and assessment, student advising, academic leadership in departments and programs, and the place of the English department in the university. NEW FOR 2027: UNDERGRADUATE ROUNDTABLES CEA invites undergraduates to enjoy the conference experience by sharing their work in flash-essay roundtable sessions. A flash essay is a highly condensed, high-impact presentation (typically 300-1000 words, or 2-5 minutes) that delivers core research findings, a specific argument, or a compelling narrative. During roundtable sessions, the speakers and audience engage in discussion with each other in more of an open conversation than in traditional panels. Learn more about roundtables here: https://cea-web.org/about-roundtables. For additional information or discussion about this topic and its panels, please contact Peter Elliott at pselliott@anderson.edu.

items.fullDescription: International Workshop: Decolonising Utopia? Literary, Cultural and Theoretical Perspectives 5-6 February, Department of English Studies, University of Cyprus Decolonial Theory (Mignolo & Walsh, 2018) emerged with the aspiration to offer a more radical critique of colonialism and imperialism than its predecessor, postcolonial theory. It has also compellingly revealed how certain strands of postcolonial thought had become compatible, if not complicit, with the very structures they set out to criticise. Concomitantly, one can observe the increasing substitution and incorporation of one tradition by the other: «Decolonisation» is the new buzzword circulating widely across the humanities and the social sciences, and the plea to decolonise is being applied to an ever-growing range of academic fields and concepts. Recently, this demand has also been directed towards utopian studies (Dinerstein 2022; Edwards 2023; Stewart 2024), emphasising the complex and multifaceted intersections between utopia and Western colonialism (Balasopoulos 2004). Besides this recent development, already since the beginning of this century, leading theorists of Utopia (Moylan 2002; Sargent 2010), partly in response to the ongoing crisis of the utopian imagination in the West, have underscored the need to articulate a postcolonial utopianism. Since then, there has been a sustained effort to broaden and challenge the Eurocentrism of the utopian tradition by including texts from diverse historical and cultural contexts and by foregrounding the utopian ideas of communities whose organisational structures differ markedly from the dominant models in the West. Decolonial critique intensifies these efforts while adding a crucial question: whether, and to what extent, can hope -as what Ernst Bloch famously described as the central affective disposition that grounds utopian imagination- undergo an epistemic decolonisation, thereby unsettling its presumed universality and leading to new conceptions of futurity and spatiality? Against this backdrop, the following question arises: how can the ambivalent relationship between utopia and decoloniality mutually enrich both fields, making utopianism a constituent element of every decolonisation process that aims to transform, rather than merely contest or critique, the existing order? This conference invites contributions that explore such questions by examining the entanglements of utopian thought, decolonial theory, and literary and cultural practices, with particular focus on the affective, epistemic, aesthetic, and political reconfigurations they engender. Possible Topics include but are not limited to: · Utopian imaginaries in colonial and postcolonial literatures and cultural productions · Indigenous, diasporic, and community-based visions of social transformation and alternative futures · Ecological imaginaries of decolonisation in green utopias and ecotopias · Utopian method and decolonial critique: theoretical and methodological reflections · Temporalities and Spatialities of decolonial utopian projects (futurity, transmodernity, cyclical or «deep» time) · The affective economies of hope, despair, and resilience in decolonial contexts · Relations between utopia, revolution, and reform in decolonial struggles · Aesthetic forms (allegory, experimental narrative, excess, non-linear structures) that reconfigure utopian and dystopian spatialities Confirmed Keynote Speakers: · Prof. Ana Cecilia Dinerstein, University of Bath · Prof. Caroline Edwards, Birkbeck, University of London Submission Guidelines · Abstracts (250-300 words) +short bio (100 words) · Deadline for applications: 6 November 2026 · Submit to: sarris.antonios@ucy.ac.cy Selected participants will present 30 minutes papers followed by discussion We intend to approach a leading journal in utopian and/or decolonial studies about publishing a special issue based on the workshop's papers. Further details will be announced in due course. The workshop is free of charge. Applicants should make the arrangements for transport and accommodation. Information on accommodation and transport will be further provided. For more information, please contact: sarris.antonios@ucy.ac.cy We look forward to receiving your proposals!

items.fullDescription: CFP: 28th Southeast Conference for Languages, Literatures, and Film (Feb 27-28, 2027) in St. Petersburg, Florida (on the University of South Florida St. Petersburg Campus) Languages and Cultures in a Changing World: Identity, Responsibility, and Justice Abstracts for papers (and panels) are now being considered. Deadline for abstracts: Nov. 16, 2026 Selected papers will be published in a post-conference anthology. To view prior publication, visit the conference website. The SCFLLF welcomes papers on all aspects of literature, theoretical and applied linguistics, culture, philosophy, cultural history, film, other popular media, second language acquisition, and language pedagogy pertaining to non-English languages (ancient and modern). We would like to encourage (but not limit) submissions addressing our conference theme: Identity, Responsibility and Justice, in its broadest understanding. Selected papers will be published in a post-conference anthology. The humanities and the study of languages are facing changing institutional and social expectations. These changes encourage us to reconsider what work we do and the people and communities our work serves. To whom and to what, are artists, scholars and teachers accountable? How do languages, literatures, films, and other forms of cultural expression preserve or challenge established narratives and structures? How do they engage with different identities? How can they help us understand the present and/or imagine different futures? What responsibilities come with teaching and learning languages as well as with studying, interpreting, and representing other cultures? This conference invites scholars working in non-English languages, literatures, film and media, cultural studies, applied and theoretical linguistics, second-language acquisition, and language pedagogy to explore these and related questions from a wide range of disciplinary, theoretical, historical, and methodological perspectives. The conference theme, Identity, Responsibility, and Justice, is deliberately broad. Responsibility may involve our relationships with students and communities, with texts and their histories, with linguistic and cultural traditions, or with the institutions in which we teach and conduct research. Or responsibility can be interrogated with regard to artists and art, in a broad sense. Justice can also be approached in diverse ways. It may involve social justice, questions of representation and recognition, historical memory, inclusion and exclusion, or access and lack thereof to language learning. Justice may also concern translation and cultural mediation or the ways in which literature, film, language, and other cultural practices engage with conflict, inequality, trauma, discrimination, displacement, and/or social change. The SCFLLF keynote speaker is Adam Schwartz (Associate Professor of Language, Culture & Society, Oregon State University). Dr. Schwartz's research addresses Spanish language education and Spanish-English multilingualisms in the U.S. He takes particular interest in intersections of language, race and racism, wherein questions of identity, responsibility and justice persist. In addition to various articles and chapters, he has authored three books. These include Spanish So White: Conversations on the Inconvenient Racism of a 'Foreign' Language Education (2023). He is also the co-author of Aquí se habla: Centering the Local and Personal in Spanish Language Education (2025) as well as Language, Identity and Justice: The Anthropolitical Worlds of Ana Celia Zentella (2026). Some suggestions of topics and their artistic representations include: identity, responsibility, and justice represented in literature, art, film, and other forms of popular media, including social media influence of film and literature on the public and private sphere reassessing the purpose and value of language teaching expressions and perceptions of trauma in response to injustice justice in utopian fictional worlds addressing and expressing identity in the language classroom questions of identity in literature, film, the arts, and other popular media responsibility issues in production and reception of artistic expressions responsibilities associated with researching and representing cultures apart or in comparison to our own the broader influence of imaginary worlds created in film, literature, the visual arts, and other forms of media on real political and personal justice language and linguistic-related topics concerning identity, responsibility, and justice other topics Please submit a proposal (of no more than 250 words) for a single paper or a full panel (max. of 3 presentations) on the conference webpage. We can only accept online submissions. Please contact Margit Grieb (grieber@usf.edu) if you have any questions.

items.fullDescription: Call for Submissions MusicTheatreDance: The Journal of the Music Theatre Dance Association Issue 1 (2027) "Imagine it" Editors: Stephanie Lim, Kathryn Edney, Hye Won Kim, Vicki Hoskins, Shiraz Biggie, and Adrienne Oehlers Imagine it: Scholarship as performance. Performance as practice. Practice as inquiry. Inquiry as pedagogy. Join us in imagining what MusicTheatreDance Journal can be. We call upon you, the scholars, educators, and practitioners in and across the performing arts, to help us envision how to break down the barriers in traditional scholarship and the communities in which we co-exist. We invite you to join us as we seek to open boundaries between fields of study in the arts, de-silo the material, and innovate the structure. We ask, how can this journal serve as a host to expand the edges of our fields and reach across the "in-betweens" to serve the varying needs of the wide range of the authorial voices in our communities? What form should scholarship take? What are the containers for scholarly rigor and thought and how can we expand and support all ideas? The Music Theatre Dance Association (MTDA) is pleased to announce a call for content for the first full issue of its flagship publication, MusicTheatreDance, intended for release in 2027. This free, open-access, peer-reviewed journal will be a multi-disciplinary space for investigations at the intersections of music, theatre, dance, and other disciplines. Seeking to disrupt traditional disciplinary boundaries, this multimodal journal will live online, playing host to both conventional scholarly essays and digital scholarship that takes other forms. We imagine a journal where a conventional 7,000-word article sits alongside choreographic analysis, a video essay, a conversation between practitioners, an interactive digital piece, an artist's notebook, or a speculative work-each reviewed according to criteria appropriate to its form rather than asking for everything to fit into the same mold. MusicTheatreDance seeks submissions across the full range of content and form, including traditional academic scholarship, artistic work, pedagogical scholarship, and other forms of research which may or may not address the theme of this first issue, "Imagine It." Our journal is poised to be a forum for timely, engaged, and innovative scholarship that fosters conversation across the field. We welcome both traditional and experimental forms of scholarly engagement that will ultimately guide the shape and scope of our three editorial sections. The editorial team offers these general categories for your submissions in the hope that the originality in form and content widens our own conceptual ideas of what our journal can be. As a starting place, your submissions can range from longer-form, more traditional, peer-reviewed article contributions (in the range of approximately 5,000-7,000 words) to non-text based submissions that engage with and build upon scholarship in the field. We are actively seeking less formal, shorter-form contributions, including and especially experiments in form and works-in-process. We are also soliciting a medley of traditional book and performance reviews, as well as less conventional and/or hybrid forms, such as interviews, dialogues, roundtables, letters to the field, commentaries, practice-as-research and pedagogical reflections, rehearsal or field documentation, annotated images, conference reports, and archive and media reviews. Submissions for the Summer 2027 issue will be accepted by November 18, 2026. Submissions will be accepted thereafter on a rolling basis for future issues, and authors/creators should submit directly via this link. The editorial team will determine the placement of work into respective sections internally. If your work takes a multimedia or nontraditional form that is not easily uploadable there, please send a query, including a complete project description and explanation of its form, in lieu of the completed work itself. Conventional texts should be prepared according to the Chicago Manual of Style. All submissions considered for the Peer-Reviewed section will be subject to anonymous evaluation. The editors of our inaugural issue (0.5) of MusicTheatreDance from Summer 2025 directed us to envision a publication that is global in its content and authorship. We continue to envision a publication that is open in every way and that does things differently. While the editorial team welcomes submissions on all applicable topics, special consideration will be given to submissions aligned with the objectives of MTDA: those which de-center white cis-heteropatriarchy. In particular, the editors encourage submissions that foreground equitable and anti-racist practices and methodologies, and/or that elevate the work of BIPOC, LGBTQIA+, disabled, women-identified, and global-majority artists and scholars. MusicTheatreDance will be published once annually online by MTDA. In addition to the sections described above, it will feature the emerging scholars' Bruce Kirle Memorial Debut Panel essays, honored each year at the annual conference of the Association for Theatre in Higher Education (ATHE), which will be edited for publication under the mentorship of a distinguished member of the field. The editorial team welcomes your questions, which you may send directly to Facilitating Editor Stephanie Lim at musictheatredancejournal@gmail.com.

items.fullDescription: Call for Essays, September 2026 Entanglements: Regimes of Extraction and The Literary Imagination of Place Co-editors: Dr. Gayathri Goel and Dr. Jennifer Horwitz The constellation of essays in this collection will focus on place-based literary works and address issues around resource extraction and ecological devastation. As the foremost cause of underdevelopment and ecological destruction in the Global South and many parts of North America, resource extraction, its resulting land loss and labor exploitation, is the occasion for this project. One of the aims of this collection is to expand "resource extraction" beyond the primary focus on extraction of fossil fuels, natural gas, and minerals and includes the commodification of any part of nature that results in impoverishment and harm without any consideration for sustainability, renewability, and justice for humans and nonhumans. The utilization and/or extraction of resources is a regular aspect of human activity for the purposes of subsistence to ensure the continued progression of human society. However, the essays in this collection will treat resource extraction as a reference to imperialist "extractivism" that depletes resources for profit, steadily impoverishing entire communities, accelerating environmental devastation, and deepening local conflicts. Central to this project is also "place" and a deep engagement with literatures that are situated in specific places around the world. As environmental issues are rooted in specific ecological practices, politics, cultures, and history, and also vary widely in nature and severity, an attention to place, then, serves as an anchor and a critical framework for complex analysis. We invite papers that can contribute to this divergent field of "place studies" by centering marginalized voices from across the globe. The accepted papers will address place-based extractivism and/or resistance to issues of exploitation of any part of an environmental community, land and habitat loss, resource scarcity, displacement/migration, collapsing interdependencies from various parts of the world, from the Pacific Islands, Asia, Africa, the Caribbean, to the Americas. The essays will use any combination of critical lenses/perspectives including, Black, Indigenous, feminist, anti-racist, anti-capitalist, decolonization thought to envision lively and liberated places for life forms beyond human and plant, animal, and avian inhabitants. Note: At this point, we are accepting essays only on African, Latin American, Pacific Ocean literatures for the collection. Please submit a 9000-word draft (including notes and citations), along with a 300-word abstract, by December 1st, 2026 to placebasedliteratures@gmail.com. Please feel free to reach out to the editors at the same email for your queries about the timeline or for any other clarifications regarding this project.

items.fullDescription: Social Inclusion, peer-reviewed journal indexed in the Social Sciences Citation Index and Scopus, welcomes new and exciting research papers for its upcoming issue "Legal Perspectives on Balancing Life and Work in the 21st Century," edited by Melanie Hack (University of Bergen) and Lisa Waddington (University of Maastricht). Submission of Abstracts: 1-15 December 2026 Submission of Full Papers: 1-15 May 2027 Publication of the Issue: June/December 2027 About the issue: Working life is undergoing its most profound transformation since the Industrial Revolution. Globalization, demographic shifts, and digitalization have already reshaped the world of work-and continue to challenge traditional models. The Covid-19 pandemic accelerated this shift, pushing work further into digital and flexible formats. This convergence of trends presents a critical challenge for Norway and other European welfare states: How to ensure safe, healthy, and inclusive work environments that support work-life balance across all life stages? Labour law and social security law may play a key role in this. Even before the pandemic, work-life balance was a priority for policymakers, reflected in the EU's European Pillar of Social Rights and the 2019 Work-life Balance Directive. Yet, legal frameworks lag behind the rapid shift of work into the private sphere. National laws must evolve to meet the demands of a more flexible, digital, and ageing workforce. Remote work, for instance, remains largely unregulated. Two key tools in promoting work-life balance and addressing inequality are: (a) flexible working arrangements and (b) access to paid leave. Equally important is ensuring protection against discrimination for those who use these tools. It has become crucial to shed light on what role tripartism and corporate social responsibility hold in achieving work-life balance. For this thematic issue, we encourage interested authors to submit proposals on relevant issues surrounding flexible work arrangements-particularly employees' autonomy over working time (e.g. right to disconnect) and location (e.g., home office, remote work, workation), and how flexible work arrangements are regulated under labour law. On this front, both country-specific analyses and cross-border perspectives are welcome. Within the EU context, special attention should be given to the implementation of the Work-Life Balance Directive and the Working Time Directive. Another important thematic area concerns leave entitlements, such as maternity, paternity, and parental leave, as well as carers' leave and annual leave. Here, the interaction between labour law and social security law is of particular interest. Finally, a perspective grounded in anti-discrimination law is also relevant-specifically, whether employees are adequately protected against discrimination when exercising rights to flexible work, paternity leave, or carers' leave. Instructions for authors: Authors interested in submitting a paper for this issue are asked to consult the journal's instructions for authors and submit their abstracts (maximum of 250 words, with a tentative title) through the abstracts system: https://www.cogitatiopress.com/app/socialinclusion/abstracts When submitting their abstracts, authors are also asked to confirm that they are aware that Social Inclusion is an open access journal with a publishing fee if the article is accepted for publication after peer-review (corresponding authors affiliated with our institutional members do not incur this fee). Open access: Readers across the globe will be able to access, share, and download this issue entirely for free. Corresponding authors affiliated with any of our institutional members (over 90 institutions worldwide) publish free of charge. Otherwise, an article processing fee will be charged to the authors to cover editorial costs. We defend that authors should not have to personally pay this fee and encourage them to check with their institutions if funds are available to cover open access publication costs. Further information about the journal's open access charges can be found here: https://www.cogitatiopress.com/socialinclusion/about/editorialPolicies#publicationFees

items.fullDescription: Call For Papers: Brecht in India - Translations, Adaptations, Performances, and Critical Perspectives Overview As a Researcher, with a focus on Kannada literature and performance, I am excited to invite submissions for an edited volume titled Brecht in India: Translations, Adaptations, Performances, and Critical Perspectives. My own research has centered on Bertolt Brecht's reception in Kannada theatre, where I uncovered an impressive 32 translations of his plays into Kannada, spanning from early post-independence efforts to contemporary reinterpretations. These findings highlight Brecht's significant influence on regional Indian theatre, blending his epic techniques with local forms like Yakshagana and modern Kannada drama. Building on this regional insight, I now seek to broaden the scope to a national perspective, gathering original research papers that examine Brecht's transcultural legacy across India's diverse linguistic, cultural, and sociopolitical landscapes. This volume will explore how Brecht's dramaturgy has been adapted to address pan-Indian issues such as caste dynamics, postcolonialism, and globalization, fostering a comprehensive dialogue on his enduring relevance. Rationale My journey into Brecht began with an in-depth study of his works in the Kannada context, revealing not only the 32 translations but also how directors and playwrights like B.V. Karanth and Prasanna have infused Brechtian alienation with indigenous elements to critique social hierarchies. This regional lens has inspired me to investigate Brecht's impact on a national scale, where his epic theatre resonates with India's multifaceted theatrical traditions-from Bengali Jatra to Tamasha . Brecht's emphasis on defamiliarization and sociopolitical engagement aligns closely with Indian folk forms that prioritize presentational styles and community involvement, making his theories particularly adaptable to addressing contemporary challenges like inequality and cultural hybridity. Nationally, Brecht's influence emerged prominently in the post-independence era, influencing Marxist theatre movements in Bengal and beyond, as seen in adaptations by figures like Utpal Dutt and Habib Tanvir. Translations of Brecht into languages such as Hindi, Bengali, and Tamil have democratized access to his works, while intercultural collaborations, including those with directors like Fritz Bennewitz, have enriched Indian performances. This volume aims to expand on such scholarship by compiling diverse perspectives, illuminating how Brecht's legacy contributes to a unified yet varied Indian theatrical identity amid global influences. Themes Contributions should address Brecht's works through a national Indian framework, drawing connections across regions. Possible topics include, but are not limited to: Relevance of Brecht in the Indian Context: Explorations of Brecht's pertinence to national sociopolitical discourses, including intersections with indigenous traditions and their role in shaping postcolonial and modern Indian identities. Translations of Brecht's Works: Analyses of translations across Indian languages (e.g., the 32 Brecht translations in Kannada, alongside those in Hindi, Bengali, Tamil, and others), focusing on linguistic nuances, cultural adaptations, and their impact on broader accessibility. Adaptations of Brechtian Drama: Studies of national adaptations, such as fusions with regional folk forms, reinterpretations by Indian playwrights like Girish Karnad or Badal Sircar, and hybrid productions that incorporate Brecht into pan-Indian narratives. Critical Views of Brechtian Performances in India: Evaluations of performances nationwide, including directorial innovations, audience responses, and critiques of how epic elements and alienation techniques appear in works by groups from various states (e.g., Kannada theatre, Bengali IPTA, or contemporary ensembles). Intercultural Exchanges and Collaborations: Examinations of cross-regional and transnational dialogues and collaborative projects that extend beyond singular linguistic or geographic boundaries. Brecht's Influence on Indian Theatre Movements: Assessments of Brecht's impact upon Indian theatre practices, including feminist, subaltern, and regionally specific perspectives. Comparative Analyses of Reception: Comparative studies of Brecht's reception across Indian languages and cultures that highlight both national commonalities and significant divergences. Submission Guidelines Abstracts: Submit a 300-500 word abstract detailing your proposed chapter, along with a brief bio (100 words) and contact information. Deadline for Abstracts: December 31, 2026. Notification of Acceptance: January 15, 2026. Full Papers: Accepted authors will submit chapters of 6,000- 8,000 words (including references) by February 31, 2027. Format: MLA 9th Edition style; Times New Roman, 12 Font Size, All submissions must be original and not under review elsewhere. Submission Email: Please send materials to brechtinindia@gmail.com with the subject line "CFP: Brecht in India Submission." I particularly welcome contributions from scholars, practitioners, and emerging researchers across India, with an emphasis on diverse regional expertise. Publication Details All accepted papers will undergo a rigorous peer-review process. The volume will be published by a reputable academic publisher to ensure scholarly rigor and global reach. The Publication of the Edited volume is anticipated in mid-2027. For any questions, please contact me at brechtinindia@gmail.com. I look forward to your insights as we collectively map Brecht's national footprint in India. Sincerely, Dr. Raghavendra H K Assistant Professor, Department of English, Jnanabharathi Campus Bangalore University

items.fullDescription: Call for Proposals The editorial and scientific board of the journal Co-herencia invites researchers, professors, and scholars affiliated with national or international institutions to submit proposals for thematic issues/dossiers, and to apply to serve as Guest Scientific Editors for Volume 25, Issue 48 (covering the period January-June 2028). Presentation and Scientific Scope of the Journal Co-herencia Co-herencia is an indexed scientific journal, published biannually, under Diamond Open Access with a CC BY 4.0 license, and edited by the School of Arts and Humanities at EAFIT University. Indexed in major international databases such as Scopus (Arts & Humanities, Q2 SJR), Co-herencia ensures methodological rigor, double-blind peer review, and high ethical publishing standards. The journal is published in Spanish, English, and Portuguese. Published without interruption since 2004, the journal aims to serve as a forum for interdisciplinary discussion on the contributions of the humanities and the arts to the shaping of a thoughtful, critical, and deliberative community. Its scope and thematic axes are concentrated mainly on: Literary Studies: Literary theory; Literary genres; Classical tradition; Hermeneutics; Canon, criticism, and history of literature in the Americas; Writing and orality; Translation; Reception; Literary creation; Semiotics; Editing studies; Journalism and literature; Applied literature. Philosophical Studies: Critical theory and social philosophy; Ethics; Political philosophy; Aesthetics; Epistemology; Philosophy of science and technology; Philosophy of mind; Cosmology; Philosophy of language; Argumentation theory; Rhetoric; Phenomenology; Philosophical hermeneutics; Ontology; Conceptual analysis; History of philosophy. Historical Studies: Historiography; Theory and philosophy of history; Methodology of history; Intellectual history; Conceptual history; Cultural history; Social and political history; History of knowledge; National and Latin American history; Global history; Colonial history; Memory and history; Historical geography and cartography; Imagination, speculation, and historical narratives. Arts: Mediality, transmediality, and intermediality; Creative industries; Musicology; History of music; Material and visual culture; Curatorship and museography; Sociology of the arts; Interartistic relations; Avant-gardes and artistic movements; Canon, criticism, and history of the arts in the Americas. Humanistic Studies in Dialogue with the Social Sciences: Critical discourse analysis; Plain language; Digital humanities; Cultural studies; Research-Creation; Philosophical and historical anthropology; Human geography; Environmental humanities; Medical humanities; Digital humanities; Public humanities; Qualitative analysis of quantitative methods; Clinical sociology; Studies on violence, peace, and reconciliation; Communication studies with a humanistic approach; Gender studies. Requirements for Submitting Proposals In keeping with international editorial best practices in the field of Arts and Humanities (diverse impact, editorial exogamy, international outreach, and analytical rigor), proposals submitted by candidates for guest editors must be presented in a single document (PDF or Word), written in Spanish, English, or Portuguese, and must include, in detail, the following five sections: Title of the thematic issue: it should be concise, clear, conceptually strong, and reflect the central problem to be addressed. Thematic presentation and theoretical grounding (500 to 1,000 words): propose a conceptual delimitation and a definition of the object of study, the core question, or the problematizing axis of the dossier. The proposal should also detail the disciplinary or interdisciplinary frameworks, indicating how the theme and approach engage with the journal's scientific scope. Justification and academic relevance (500 to 1,000 words): include a synthesis of the state of the art and a clear account of the novelty and relevance of the proposal within the contemporary debate in the arts and humanities. This section should ideally state the potential impact and interest the issue will generate within the international research community. Scientific biography of the prospective guest editors: a team of two to three guest editors with diverse institutional affiliations is recommended. For each team member, please indicate: full name, current institutional affiliation, highest academic degree, ORCID iD, and a summary (max. 300 words) of their research lines, ongoing projects, and recent publications in the thematic area of the proposal. List of prospective authors and articles: as evidence of the commitment to attracting original manuscripts, this section of the proposal must list between 3 and 6 potential or pre-invited authors of recognized standing or relevant emerging trajectory for the thematic issue. For each anticipated contribution, please provide: the author's full name, institutional affiliation, tentative article title, and a brief abstract (100-200 words). All manuscripts resulting from the call for the selected proposal must undergo double-blind peer review. Guest editors commit to actively participating in the preselection of manuscripts, suggesting qualified reviewers, and drafting a presentation/introduction for the dossier. Timeline for the Open Call and the Editorial Process Opening of the call for thematic issue proposals: September 1, 2026. Deadline for submission of thematic issue proposals: January 10, 2027. Evaluation of proposals by the scientific board and notification of results: January 25, 2027. Public launch of the call for the selected proposal: January 31, 2027. Deadline for submission of articles for the thematic dossier: May 31, 2027. Peer review and revision process: June-November 2027. Early publication of revised articles: October 2027-January 2028. Copyediting, XML-JATS markup, and digital layout: November 2027-February 2028. Official publication (Vol. 25, No. 48, January-June 2028): February-March 2028. How to Submit Proposals Complete proposals must be submitted electronically to the journal's official email (co-herencia@eafit.edu.co) or processed through the Co-herencia journal's OJS (Open Journal System) platform, attaching the document (PDF or Word) with the required information, using the subject line "Application for Thematic Dossier Vol. 25-48 - [Short title of the proposal]." items.fullDescription: In his seminal and final film Black Is…Black Ain't , the documentarian Marlon Riggs utilizes a pot of gumbo to articulate his thesis that Blackness necessitates an identity built on multiplicity, complication, and depth, a production requiring expansiveness in its sustained attention (Riggs 1995). Such a vision contests and destabilizes narratives depicted within the film that sought to limit Black identities and identifications, and it cuts against the second half of his title, which suggests Blackness in terms of negation, evasion, and minimization. The title to this conference continues a conversation with Riggs and also with Ralph Ellison, Ama Ata Aidoo, Toni Morrison, Stuart Hall, and centuries of international Black thought. By doubling down on the "is" and considering contradictory, harmonious, and contrapuntal accounts of the many ways Blackness is and can be, the Gregory J. Hampton Graduate English Student Association hopes to encourage a maximalist exchange with its conference, being held March 25-26, 2027, as a contemplation of storytelling and its connections to productions and identities of Blackness. We also seek to do commemorative work as we honor the career of Dr. Jimisha Relerford, a graduate of our program and member of the Howard community who passed recently. Her dissertation broke critical ground in its study of Black women's satire. We thus encourage the submission of papers about Black satire, especially Black women's work in the genre. Writers such as Leone Ross, Danzy Senna, Fran Ross, and Zadie Smith, all of whom were discussed in Dr. Relerford's dissertation, utilize satire to comment on and transform notions of Blackness. We hope to continue Dr. Relerford's work by contemplating how storytellers work within this genre to talk about identity. We additionally encourage work on Afrofuturism and speculative Black texts in reference to our organization's namesake, a pillar in Afrofuturist study. In addition to recognizing the intellectual impacts of Drs. Relerford and Hampton, this conference serves as a milestone, marking the tenth conference our organization has hosted in honor of Black literary study. Given Black academia and HBCUs's influence on identity and storytelling around it, we also welcome papers grounded in studies of scholarly impacts on identity as seen in multimodal narratives, productions, protests, and criticism. We additionally invite papers in the following areas that intersect with identity and identification study in story: African Studies African-American Studies Caribbean Studies Disability Studies Ecocriticism and Ecopoetics Diaspora, Ethnicity, and Migration Studies Food Studies Hip Hop Humor Literary History Protest and Rhetoric Queer Studies Television and Film To submit a paper or panel to our conference, please email an abstract of 250-300 words to gesasecretary@gmail.com no later than January 15, 2027. Include in your email, your name, affiliation, contact information, and a brief biographical blurb.

items.fullDescription: CALL FOR PAPERS The Politics of Care in Higher Education: Pedagogies, Communities, and Institutional Tensions Eds. Gretta Sayers, Dominique Hétu, and Mousumi Majumder This edited collection offers a timely contribution to the growing body of scholarship on care in higher education (Child & Marvel, 2023; Johnston, 2024; Evans, 2025; Boden et al., 2026). Moving beyond celebratory narratives that romanticize care, treat it as inherently benevolent, or present it as a natural and uncomplicated good, this volume approaches care as a complex and contested practice shaped by institutional structures, power relations, material conditions, and unequal distributions of labour. It examines how care operates simultaneously as a pedagogical ethic, relational practice, and institutional discourse, while foregrounding the tensions and contradictions that emerge in its enactment in higher education. We seek contributions that examine both the transformative possibilities and the political contradictions of care in academic life, engaging urgent concerns surrounding precarity, burnout, institutional rhetoric, and collective responsibility while offering grounded and theoretically rigorous pathways for reimagining academic communities. Guided by an editorial team working across science, arts, and music, the volume approaches care as a question that exceeds disciplinary boundaries and conventional academic forms. We welcome interdisciplinary contributions exploring pedagogies of care in academia as relational, political, ethical, and institutional practices, and particularly encourage critical perspectives attentive to the tensions between care as transformative praxis and care as institutional discourse. In keeping with this interdisciplinary and expansive orientation, we welcome not only scholarly analysis but also contributions that engage pedagogical and institutional questions through research-creation, creative and arts-based methodologies, embodied and relational inquiry, and other forms of knowledge-making attentive to care, reciprocity, and collective responsibility. Possible topics may include, but are not limited to: Communities of Practice, Solidarity, and Collective Care Focus on the relationships, networks, and collective structures through which care is enacted, sustained, and negotiated within and beyond academic institutions. Contributions may critically examine communities of practice, mentorship, solidarity, belonging, and collective responses to precarity, exclusion, and institutional change. Communities of practice as spaces of relational learning and mutual support Collective care and solidarity within academic communities Faculty, staff, student, and intergenerational communities of care Mentorship, sponsorship, and peer-support networks Community-based and grassroots care practices Communities of resistance and alternative academic cultures Care infrastructures within and beyond institutions Transnational, intercultural, and multilingual communities of practice Critical and Decolonial Theorizations of Care Feminist, decolonial, anti-racist, Indigenous, disability, queer, and intersectional approaches to care Care as relational, political, ethical, and collective practice Relational accountability, reciprocity, and responsibility Distinctions and tensions between care, compassion, empathy, wellness, and support Decolonizing care and questioning dominant or universalized understandings of care Care, power, and the politics of recognition and belonging Care, Institutions, and Structural Conditions Who is responsible for care? items.fullDescription: Punk has never stayed where it was put. Emerging from the economic, political and cultural upheavals of the 1970s, punk became music, style, attitude, subculture, political language and cultural mythology. From London, New York, Sydney, Belfast, Berlin, Tokyo and Jakarta, punk travelled rapidly while taking radically different local forms. It transformed music and fashion, challenged conventions of gender and sexuality, generated distinctive visual and material cultures, and provided a language through which alienation, anger, resistance and belonging could be expressed. Yet punk has also become something it once appeared determined to resist: heritage, commodity and nostalgia. Torn clothing and safety pins entered high fashion. Punk records became collectors' items. Posters and fanzines entered museums and archives. Bands once associated with underground scenes became canonical figures in popular music history. Punk aesthetics circulate through advertising, television, film and social media, while successive generations continue to rediscover, appropriate and reinvent punk. The Popular Culture Research Network (PopCRN) invites proposals for an interdisciplinary conference exploring punk as a major formation in popular culture, from its historical emergence to its contemporary afterlives. The conference asks what happens when punk moves beyond the scene and becomes popular culture. How has punk been represented, remembered, commercialised, institutionalised and reinvented? Who has been included in dominant histories of punk, and who has been marginalised? How do histories of punk change when examined through race, class, gender, sexuality, disability, age, place and nationality? Can punk retain oppositional force once its sounds, images and objects circulate through mainstream culture? Papers might examine punk through music, film, television, fashion, photography, art, literature, comics, performance, celebrity, journalism, advertising, material culture, museums, archives, digital culture, fandom or everyday life. Possible topics include: Origins, scenes and histories: CBGB and New York punk; London and the Sex Pistols; The Clash and political punk; Ramones and the aesthetics of speed and simplicity; Patti Smith and punk poetics; Australian punk and bands such as The Saints and Radio Birdman; local scenes and regional histories; punk behind the Iron Curtain; punk outside Britain and the United States; post punk, hardcore, anarcho punk and other transformations of the form. Race, class and politics: punk and working class identity; unemployment and economic decline; anti establishment politics; Rock Against Racism; punk and anti fascism; race and the whiteness of punk histories; Black punk; Indigenous punk; migration and diaspora; colonialism and postcolonial punk; nationalism and punk; policing, surveillance and censorship; punk as protest. Gender, sexuality and the body: women in punk; Siouxsie Sioux, Poly Styrene, Debbie Harry, Patti Smith and other punk icons; queercore; punk masculinities; Riot Grrrl; sexuality and transgression; beauty, ugliness and bodily refusal; hair, tattoos, piercing and bodily modification; punk ageing and the changing punk body. Fashion, style and material culture: Vivienne Westwood and Malcolm McLaren; bondage trousers, leather jackets, ripped clothing and safety pins; DIY fashion; hairstyles and cosmetics; punk typography and graphic design; album covers; badges and patches; record collecting; fanzines, flyers and posters; punk bedrooms, clubs and record shops; the movement of punk style from the street to the runway. Sound, Performance and the Punk Aesthetic: noise, distortion, speed and brevity; amateurism and anti virtuosity; screaming and vocal performance; three chord aesthetics; live performance; pogoing and moshing; stage violence and confrontation; audience participation; punk humour, obscenity and provocation; the aesthetics of ugliness and deliberate failure. Global Punk: punk in Aotearoa New Zealand, Japan, Indonesia, China, Eastern Europe, Latin America, Africa and the Middle East; punk under authoritarian regimes; Indigenous punk; postcolonial punk; migration and diaspora; translation and localisation; how punk changes as it moves between cultures. Punk on screen: Jubilee (1978); The Great Rock 'n' Roll Swindle (1980); Sid and Nancy (1986); Dogs in Space (1986); The Decline of Western Civilization (1981); This Is England (2006); punk documentaries and biopics; fictional punks; punk television; punk soundtracks; punk as shorthand for danger, rebellion and social disorder. Media, technology and DIY culture: independent labels; pirate and community radio; cassette culture; photocopying and the fanzine; punk photography; alternative publishing; bootlegs; punk journalism; online archives; social media; streaming and the digital rediscovery of punk; DIY culture before and after the internet. Punk, commerce and contradiction: punk and the music industry; selling rebellion; punk in advertising; luxury fashion and punk aesthetics; celebrity punks; authenticity and accusations of selling out; punk merchandise; nostalgia markets; reunion tours; anniversaries and reissues; punk as brand. Punk celebrity: Sid Vicious as punk celebrity; Debbie Harry and celebrity femininity; Johnny Rotten and the transformation of punk notoriety into media celebrity; punk autobiography; celebrity ageing; the punk icon as commodity. Memory, heritage and afterlives: museums and exhibitions; archives and personal collections; punk heritage tourism; oral histories; documentaries and retrospectives; anniversaries; canon formation; forgotten punk histories; ageing punks; intergenerational fandom; the preservation of ephemeral culture; whose punk becomes history? After punk: post punk, goth, hardcore, grunge, emo and alternative music; Riot Grrrl; punk's influence on fashion and visual culture; punk aesthetics in contemporary protest; new global punk scenes; TikTok and punk revivalism; Gen Z encounters with punk; the continuing circulation of DIY and anti establishment cultures. Please submit abstracts (200 words) and author details via our online portal by 31 July 2027. Notification of abstract acceptance is 31 August 2027. Registration is free. The conference is welcoming of early career researchers, postgraduates, Indigenous scholars, people with diverse identities, and industry experts or food practitioners. Please send any queries to popcrn@une.edu.au · Submit here - https://unesurveys.au1.qualtrics.com/jfe/form/SV_8jjzaWnS732QsFE · Register here - https://unesurveys.au1.qualtrics.com/jfe/form/SV_7TGWUYZidtlxVLU
